henry_vii.name: Henry VII
henry_vii.desc:
Founder of the Tudor dynasty, who took the throne after defeating Richard III at Bosworth in August 1485. His claim was weak, resting on the Beaufort line and on conquest, and he dated his reign from the day before the battle so that those who had fought against him were technically traitors.

He restored royal finances through bonds, recognisances and fines administered by Empson and Dudley, and used the Council and the prerogative courts to bring over-mighty subjects to heel. His children's marriages secured alliances with Spain and Scotland.

Two serious impostures, by Lambert Simnel and Perkin Warbeck, occupied the first fourteen years of the reign. He died in 1509 leaving a solvent treasury and an undisputed succession, the first English king in a century to manage both.

henry_viii.name: Henry VIII
henry_viii.desc:
King from 1509, who broke with papal authority in order to annul his first marriage and was declared Supreme Head of the Church of England by statute in 1534.

His six marriages produced three legitimate children by three wives; two queens were executed and two marriages annulled. The dissolution of the monasteries transferred perhaps a fifth of England's landed wealth to the crown and then to its purchasers, and the legislation of the 1530s made parliament the instrument through which the church settlement was made and remade.

Doctrinally he remained conservative, retaining the mass and executing both Catholic loyalists and evangelical reformers. Expensive wars with France and Scotland and the debasement of the coinage consumed the monastic windfall, leaving his son's government in serious difficulty.

edward_vi.name: Edward VI
edward_vi.desc:
Henry VIII's only surviving legitimate son, born in 1537, who came to the throne at nine and died at fifteen.

Government passed first to his uncle Edward Seymour as Lord Protector and then, after the risings of 1549, to John Dudley as Lord President of the Council. Under both the English Church moved decisively toward reformed doctrine: images were removed, clerical marriage permitted, chantries dissolved, and the Books of Common Prayer of 1549 and 1552 imposed by statute.

Well educated and firmly committed to the new religion, he drew up a Device for the Succession in his last months excluding both half-sisters in favour of Jane Grey. He died in July 1553, probably of tuberculosis.

mary_i.name: Mary I
mary_i.desc:
Daughter of Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon, who took the throne in July 1553 after popular support collapsed the attempt to install Jane Grey — the one moment in the century when the legitimate heir prevailed against the men holding the capital.

She reversed her brother's religious settlement, restored papal authority through Cardinal Pole, and revived the heresy laws under which around 280 Protestants were burned between 1555 and 1558. Her marriage to Philip II of Spain in 1554 was widely unpopular and provoked Wyatt's rising.

Her administration carried through useful reform of the coinage and the customs, work her successor retained. She died childless in November 1558, months after the loss of Calais, England's last continental possession.

elizabeth_i.name: Elizabeth I
elizabeth_i.desc:
The last Tudor monarch, who reigned from 1558 for forty-five years and never married, using the prospect of her marriage as a diplomatic instrument for two decades.

The settlement of 1559 established a church reformed in doctrine and episcopal in structure, deliberately ambiguous on the eucharist so that most consciences could conform. She resisted pressure from her own councillors and parliaments to name a successor, to intervene more aggressively abroad, and to proceed against Mary, Queen of Scots.

Her reign saw the excommunication of 1570, the Catholic plots that followed, war with Spain from 1585, the defeat of the Armada, and a long and costly conflict in Ireland. It also saw the commercial playhouse, the first English colonial ventures, and a court culture that made her image into a governing instrument.

jane_grey.name: Lady Jane Grey
jane_grey.desc:
Great-granddaughter of Henry VII through his daughter Mary, and a committed Protestant of unusual learning, proclaimed queen in July 1553 under a scheme by the Duke of Northumberland to preserve the religious settlement.

She had been married to Northumberland's son Guildford Dudley weeks earlier. Her title rested on Edward VI's Device for the Succession, which had no statutory force against Henry VIII's will and the Act of Succession.

Support collapsed within nine days as Mary raised East Anglia and the Council in London changed sides. Jane was held in the Tower and executed in February 1554, aged about seventeen, after Wyatt's rebellion made her continued existence a danger to the new regime.

james_vi_i.name: James VI and I
james_vi_i.desc:
King of Scots from the age of thirteen months, after his mother's forced abdication in 1567, and from March 1603 the first Stuart king of England.

His minority was governed by a succession of regents and his upbringing directed by Protestant tutors including George Buchanan. He established a working control over the Scottish nobility and kirk, and wrote on kingship in Basilikon Doron and The Trew Law of Free Monarchies.

His accession united the two crowns in one person, though not the two kingdoms, and ended the Tudor line. The claim rested on descent from Henry VII through Margaret Tudor, and had been quietly prepared for years by Robert Cecil.

elizabeth_of_york.name: Elizabeth of York
elizabeth_of_york.desc:
Daughter of Edward IV and Elizabeth Woodville, and the senior surviving Yorkist heir after the disappearance of her brothers in 1483.

Her marriage to Henry VII in January 1486, promised publicly before Bosworth, joined the Yorkist and Lancastrian claims and gave the new dynasty a legitimacy its founder's own descent could not supply. The union was represented afterwards in the Tudor rose.

She was the mother of Arthur, Margaret, Henry VIII and Mary, and by contemporary account the marriage became an affectionate one. She died in the Tower in February 1503, shortly after childbirth, on her thirty-seventh birthday.

margaret_beaufort.name: Margaret Beaufort
margaret_beaufort.desc:
Henry VII's mother, whose descent from John of Gaunt through the Beaufort line carried the Lancastrian claim her son advanced in 1485. She was thirteen at his birth and was widowed before it.

Through three subsequent marriages, the last to Lord Stanley, she remained at or near the centre of political affairs and was involved in the negotiations with the Woodvilles that preceded Bosworth. Under her son she held an unusual legal independence for a married woman, styling herself Margaret R.

She endowed professorships at both universities, founded Christ's and St John's Colleges at Cambridge, and was a patron of Caxton and Wynkyn de Worde. She outlived Henry VII by two months.

arthur_tudor.name: Arthur, Prince of Wales
arthur_tudor.desc:
Henry VII's eldest son, born at Winchester in September 1486 and named to attach the new dynasty to British legend. He was created Prince of Wales at three and raised from the cradle as the heir.

He married Catherine of Aragon in November 1501 in a ceremony of deliberate magnificence, sealing the alliance with Spain that his father had spent years negotiating, and the couple were sent to hold the Welsh Marches from Ludlow.

He died there the following April, probably of the sweating sickness. Whether the marriage had been consummated in those five months could not be established, and the question became central to Henry VIII's case for annulment thirty years later.

margaret_tudor.name: Margaret Tudor
margaret_tudor.desc:
Henry VII's elder daughter, married to James IV of Scotland in 1503 under the Treaty of Perpetual Peace, which was intended to settle the northern border and did so for ten years.

Widowed at Flodden in 1513, she was left regent for her infant son James V, lost the regency through remarriage to the Earl of Angus, and spent the following two decades manoeuvring between pro-English and pro-French factions in Scotland, including a contested divorce.

Her descendants included Mary, Queen of Scots and James VI. Through her the Stuart line inherited the English throne in 1603, an outcome Henry VII is said to have anticipated and accepted.

catherine_of_aragon.name: Catherine of Aragon
catherine_of_aragon.desc:
Daughter of Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile, widow of Prince Arthur, and queen to Henry VIII for twenty-four years from 1509.

She acted as regent during the French campaign of 1513, when English forces defeated the Scots at Flodden, and was a serious patron of humanist learning; Vives wrote on female education for her daughter at her request. Of six pregnancies only Mary survived infancy.

From 1527 she refused to accept that her marriage was invalid, maintaining that her union with Arthur had never been consummated and appealing the case to Rome. Her resistance, supported by her nephew the emperor, prolonged the proceedings for six years and contributed directly to the break with Rome. She died at Kimbolton in January 1536.

anne_boleyn.name: Anne Boleyn
anne_boleyn.desc:
Queen to Henry VIII from January 1533 and mother of Elizabeth I, raised partly at the French court and associated at the English one with evangelical reform and the circulation of prohibited books.

Her refusal of the position of mistress prolonged the king's pursuit for some six years, during which the annulment case and then the break with Rome proceeded. She promoted reformist clerics to bishoprics and quarrelled with Cromwell over the destination of monastic revenues.

She was arrested in May 1536 and tried with five men, including her brother, on charges of adultery, incest and conspiring the king's death. All were convicted and executed; historians now generally regard the accusations as unfounded. Anne was beheaded within the Tower on 19 May by a swordsman brought from Calais.

jane_seymour.name: Jane Seymour
jane_seymour.desc:
Henry VIII's third queen, married in May 1536 within days of Anne Boleyn's execution, and the only one of his wives to bear a son who survived infancy.

She had served in the households of both previous queens. Conservative in religion, she appealed unsuccessfully to the king on behalf of the northern rebels during the Pilgrimage of Grace, and worked to have Mary restored to favour and to the succession. Her motto was Bound to Obey and Serve.

Edward was born at Hampton Court in October 1537 after a long labour, and Jane died there twelve days later of complications following the birth. Henry directed that he be buried beside her, and was.

anne_of_cleves.name: Anne of Cleves
anne_of_cleves.desc:
Sister of the Duke of Cleves, married to Henry VIII in January 1540 in a match arranged by Cromwell to align England with the Protestant German princes at a moment of Catholic diplomatic threat.

The alliance lost its purpose almost immediately as the international situation shifted, and Henry sought release. The marriage was annulled in July on grounds of a prior betrothal and non-consummation; Anne agreed without contest, and the minister who had arranged it was executed the same month.

She was granted Richmond, Bletchingley and Hever, the precedence of the King's Sister, and an independent income. She remained in England on good terms with the royal children, attended Mary I's coronation, and outlived every other wife, dying in 1557.

catherine_howard.name: Catherine Howard
catherine_howard.desc:
A niece of the Duke of Norfolk, brought to court in the household of Anne of Cleves and married to Henry VIII in July 1540, when she was probably about seventeen and he was forty-nine.

She had been raised in the crowded household of the Dowager Duchess of Norfolk with little supervision, and relationships there before the marriage were later brought in evidence, along with meetings with Thomas Culpeper during it, arranged with the help of Lady Rochford.

Cranmer passed the allegations to the king in a letter in November 1541. A new act made it treasonable for an unchaste woman to marry a king, and she was condemned by attainder rather than trial and executed in February 1542.

catherine_parr.name: Catherine Parr
catherine_parr.desc:
Henry VIII's sixth and last queen, married in July 1543, a twice-widowed noblewoman of evangelical sympathies and considerable learning.

She acted as regent during the king's French campaign of 1544, and was instrumental in the Act of Succession that restored Mary and Elizabeth to the line of succession and in assembling the reformist tutors who taught the younger children. She published Prayers or Meditations in 1545 and The Lamentation of a Sinner in 1547, the first English queen to publish under her own name.

Conservatives at court came close to procuring her arrest for heresy in 1546; she talked her way out of it. She married Thomas Seymour within months of the king's death and died in childbirth in September 1548.

mary_queen_scots.name: Mary, Queen of Scots
mary_queen_scots.desc:
Queen of Scots from the age of six days on the death of James V in 1542, raised in France from the age of five and briefly queen consort there through her marriage to Francis II.

As a granddaughter of Margaret Tudor she was the senior Catholic claimant to the English throne, and her quartering of the English arms in 1559 was never forgiven. Returning to Scotland in 1561, she governed with some success until the murder of Darnley and her marriage to Bothwell destroyed her support.

Deposed and forced to abdicate in 1567, she fled to England in 1568 expecting assistance and was held in custody for nineteen years. Successive plots were made in her name, and after the Babington conspiracy she was tried at Fotheringhay and executed there in February 1587.

thomas_wolsey.name: Thomas Wolsey
thomas_wolsey.desc:
The son of an Ipswich tradesman, who rose through the church to become Archbishop of York, cardinal, papal legate and Lord Chancellor, directing English government and diplomacy for some fifteen years.

He handled the routine of administration so completely that the young king could leave it to him, and used the legatine authority to reform monasteries and fund his colleges at Ipswich and Oxford. In Star Chamber he pursued enclosure and the abuses of powerful men, which made him enemies among the nobility.

His diplomacy aimed at holding the balance between France and the Empire, and produced the Treaty of London and the Field of the Cloth of Gold. His failure to secure the annulment ended his career in 1529; he died at Leicester in 1530 travelling south to face a charge of treason.

thomas_cromwell.name: Thomas Cromwell
thomas_cromwell.desc:
Henry VIII's chief minister from the early 1530s, who had served Wolsey before him and survived his fall by remaining useful in the Commons.

He supplied the legal machinery of the break with Rome, carrying the supremacy, the treason act and the dissolution through parliament rather than by prerogative, and as Vicegerent in Spirituals he exercised the new authority on the king's behalf, ranking above the archbishops. He reorganised royal administration around departments of state and ordered the keeping of parish registers.

He promoted the English Bible and protected evangelical preachers. The failure of the Cleves marriage gave his conservative enemies their opening; he was arrested at the Council table in June 1540, attainted without trial, and executed. Henry was blaming his councillors for the loss within a year.

thomas_more.name: Thomas More
thomas_more.desc:
Humanist scholar, lawyer and author of Utopia, a friend of Erasmus and one of the leading figures of English learning, who became Speaker of the Commons and then Lord Chancellor in 1529.

He was a vigorous opponent of Lutheranism, writing extensively against Tyndale and pursuing heretical books and their importers with a severity his later reputation tends to obscure. He resigned the chancellorship in May 1532, the day after the clergy submitted to the king.

He declined to swear the oath of succession and would not give reasons, holding that the law could not punish silence. Convicted of treason largely on evidence given by Richard Rich, which he denied, he was beheaded on Tower Hill in July 1535 and canonised four centuries later.

william_cecil.name: William Cecil, Lord Burghley
william_cecil.desc:
Created Lord Burghley in 1571, he served Elizabeth I as Principal Secretary and then Lord Treasurer for forty years and was the central figure in her administration from its first day to his death in 1598.

He managed the religious settlement through a hostile House of Lords in 1559, oversaw the recoinage, the poor law and the regulation of trade, and built an intelligence and paper machine that made the Council genuinely informed. He argued consistently for supporting Protestant causes abroad and against the queen's instinct for delay.

He regarded Mary, Queen of Scots as an unacceptable risk from the moment she entered England, drafted the Bond of Association, and pressed the trial through. He trained his younger son Robert to succeed him, and largely did.

robert_cecil.name: Robert Cecil
robert_cecil.desc:
Burghley's younger son, small and physically slight in a court that valued display, trained in government from boyhood and doing the Secretary's work for years before he was given the title in 1596.

He built his father's machine into an instrument he controlled personally, and by the last years of the reign managed access to the queen almost entirely. His rivalry with Essex was fought over patronage and policy, and he won it largely by remaining in London while Essex went to Ireland.

From about 1601 he conducted a secret correspondence in cipher with James VI, coaching him on how to approach English opinion, so that the accession of March 1603 was settled within hours. He served James as Earl of Salisbury until 1612.

francis_walsingham.name: Francis Walsingham
francis_walsingham.desc:
Elizabeth I's Principal Secretary from 1573, a committed Protestant who had spent Mary's reign in exile and served as ambassador in Paris during the St Bartholomew's Day massacre.

He built an intelligence network reaching across France, Spain, Italy and the Low Countries, employing cipher specialists, double agents and interceptors, and funded a great deal of it himself. He argued continually for a more assertive Protestant foreign policy than the queen would authorise, and for the removal of Mary Stuart.

His control of the channel through which Mary's correspondence passed produced the evidence that convicted her in 1586. He supported colonial and exploratory ventures and the Sidney circle, and died in 1590 heavily in debt.

edward_seymour.name: Edward Seymour, Duke of Somerset
edward_seymour.desc:
Edward VI's elder uncle, created Duke of Somerset and Lord Protector in 1547 by setting aside the balanced regency council named in Henry VIII's will.

He advanced Protestant reform through the first Act of Uniformity and pursued a war in Scotland intended to force the marriage of Edward to Mary, Queen of Scots; the victory at Pinkie was followed by an expensive and futile garrison policy that drove the Scots into French arms.

Sympathetic to complaints about enclosure, he was blamed for encouraging the risings of 1549 in the West Country and East Anglia. Removed from the Protectorate that autumn by John Dudley, briefly restored to the Council, he was executed in January 1552 on a charge of felony.

john_dudley.name: John Dudley, Duke of Northumberland
john_dudley.desc:
Son of Henry VII's unpopular financial agent Edmund Dudley, and a capable soldier and admiral who suppressed Kett's rebellion in 1549 and then displaced Somerset.

Created Duke of Northumberland, he governed for Edward VI as Lord President of the Council rather than as Protector, ended the Scottish and French wars, began to repair the debased coinage, and drove through the more sharply reformed Prayer Book of 1552.

He married his son Guildford to Jane Grey in May 1553 and supported the Device that diverted the succession from Mary. When the country moved to Mary he abandoned the attempt at Cambridge, and he was executed in August 1553 after conforming publicly to Catholicism to no effect.

christopher_hatton.name: Christopher Hatton
christopher_hatton.desc:
A courtier who came to Elizabeth's notice in the 1560s, reportedly through his dancing at a court masque, and rose steadily through the household to become Lord Chancellor in 1587 despite limited legal training.

He was one of the courtier-officials the queen preferred to keep close, managing crown business in the Commons, sitting on the commission that tried Mary, Queen of Scots, and speaking for the government on the religious settlement against Puritan pressure.

He invested substantially in Drake's circumnavigation, and Drake renamed his ship the Golden Hind during the voyage after the hind in Hatton's arms. He built Holdenby House as a house fit to receive the queen, and died in 1591 owing her a large sum she had lent him.

francis_bacon.name: Francis Bacon
francis_bacon.desc:
Lawyer, member of parliament, essayist and philosopher, nephew of Lord Burghley, who argued that natural knowledge should be built by systematic observation and experiment rather than deduction from authority.

He sought office under Elizabeth persistently and with limited success, having offended her early by opposing a subsidy in the Commons. He was a client of Essex, who gave him an estate when he could not obtain him a post, and then appeared for the crown at Essex's trial and wrote the official account justifying the verdict.

Under James he rose to Lord Chancellor before falling in 1621 on charges of taking bribes. The Advancement of Learning and the Novum Organum set out the method that later natural philosophers took up.

robert_dudley.name: Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester
robert_dudley.desc:
Created Earl of Leicester in 1564, he was the son and grandson of executed men, had been imprisoned in the Tower at the same time as Elizabeth in 1554, and was her closest courtier from her accession.

Marriage between them was widely expected in the early 1560s and became impossible after the death of his wife Amy Robsart in 1560 in circumstances that could not be publicly cleared. He remained at the centre of the court for thirty years, a patron of Protestant clergy, of players and of Spenser.

He commanded the expedition to the Netherlands in 1585 and accepted the title of Governor-General there without the queen's permission, which she never entirely forgave. He organised the Tilbury camp in 1588 and died weeks later; she kept his last letter until her death.

robert_devereux.name: Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex
robert_devereux.desc:
Second Earl of Essex, stepson of Leicester and son of Lettice Knollys, who arrived at court in the mid-1580s and became the queen's last great favourite.

Popular in the country and with the soldiers, he pressed constantly for military commands and an aggressive war policy, made his reputation at Cadiz in 1596, and quarrelled repeatedly with the Cecils over patronage and with the queen over both. His following made him the focus of everyone excluded from the Cecil interest.

Appointed to command in Ireland in 1599 with the largest army of the reign, he negotiated a truce with Tyrone and returned without leave. Confined and stripped of his revenues, he attempted a rising in the City in February 1601 and was executed at the Tower.

walter_raleigh.name: Walter Raleigh
walter_raleigh.desc:
Soldier, courtier, poet, coloniser and writer, from a Devon gentry family, who served in France and Ireland before arriving at court about 1581 and rising rapidly in the queen's favour.

He received monopolies, the wine licence and large Irish estates, promoted the Virginia voyages that produced the Roanoke settlements, and gathered around him a circle including Harriot and Marlowe that attracted rumours of irreligion. His secret marriage to Elizabeth Throckmorton in 1592 cost him the favour permanently.

He led expeditions to Guiana in search of a rich interior kingdom. Convicted of treason on thin evidence at James's accession, he spent thirteen years in the Tower writing his History of the World, and was executed in 1618 after a final Guiana voyage broke the peace with Spain.

philip_sidney.name: Philip Sidney
philip_sidney.desc:
Courtier, soldier and writer, nephew of Leicester and son of the Lord Deputy of Ireland, educated at Shrewsbury and Oxford and widely travelled in Protestant Europe.

He wrote Astrophil and Stella, the first substantial English sonnet sequence, the prose romance Arcadia, and the Defence of Poesy, none of them printed in his lifetime; circulation in manuscript was the normal mode for a gentleman writer. He argued against the proposed French marriage in a letter to the queen and was banished from court for it.

He was appointed Governor of Flushing in 1585 and wounded in a skirmish near Zutphen in September 1586, dying at Arnhem some weeks later. His funeral was a major public occasion and his reputation afterwards was as the model Protestant gentleman.

charles_brandon.name: Charles Brandon, Duke of Suffolk
charles_brandon.desc:
Created Duke of Suffolk in 1514, he was Henry VIII's companion in the tiltyard and one of the few men who could speak frankly to him and survive it, though he came from a family of no great standing.

Sent to France in 1515 to escort the king's widowed sister Mary home, he married her there without permission, an offence that could have cost him his head; he was fined heavily instead and restored to favour within months.

He served on campaigns in France and commanded royal forces against the Pilgrimage of Grace in 1536, negotiating and then enforcing the settlement in Lincolnshire. He remained close to the king for thirty years and died in 1545, the last of Henry's early companions still standing.

thomas_howard_norfolk3.name: Thomas Howard, 3rd Duke of Norfolk
thomas_howard_norfolk3.desc:
Third Duke of Norfolk, the leading conservative peer of Henry VIII's reign, uncle to Anne Boleyn and Catherine Howard, and the chief representative of the old nobility against the new men of the 1530s.

He commanded against the Pilgrimage of Grace in 1536, promising a pardon and a parliament he had no authority to grant and executing the leaders once the rebels dispersed. He presided at the trials of both his nieces and took a leading part in the destruction of Cromwell in 1540.

His own family fell in 1546 when his son the Earl of Surrey quartered the royal arms. Condemned for treason in January 1547, he escaped execution because Henry VIII died the night before, spent Edward's reign in the Tower, and was released by Mary.

thomas_howard_norfolk4.name: Thomas Howard, 4th Duke of Norfolk
thomas_howard_norfolk4.desc:
Fourth Duke of Norfolk and the only duke in England under Elizabeth, raised as a Protestant after his father's execution, with John Foxe among his tutors.

Three times widowed and immensely wealthy, he was persuaded from 1569 that marrying Mary, Queen of Scots would settle the succession and restore the old nobility to influence. The scheme was known to much of the Council before it reached the queen, and he was sent to the Tower and then released to house arrest.

He was drawn back in through Ridolfi's plan for a Spanish landing, and the incriminating correspondence was found at Howard House. Convicted in January 1572, he was executed in June after Elizabeth had signed and revoked the warrant three times.

bess_of_hardwick.name: Bess of Hardwick
bess_of_hardwick.desc:
Married four times, each time advantageously, she accumulated one of the largest private fortunes in Elizabethan England through jointures, careful estate management and lead and coal interests.

Her fourth husband, the Earl of Shrewsbury, was for fifteen years the custodian of Mary, Queen of Scots; the burden and expense of that charge, and Bess's own accusations about it, wrecked the marriage. She served in the privy chamber and survived several spells of disgrace.

She built Chatsworth and then Hardwick Hall, and her needlework and building accounts are among the fullest records of an Elizabethan household. Her granddaughter Arbella Stuart had a claim to the throne, which brought Bess both prominence and lasting official suspicion.

lettice_knollys.name: Lettice Knollys
lettice_knollys.desc:
A cousin of Elizabeth I through the Boleyn line, daughter of Sir Francis Knollys, and a woman of the queen's own kin who served in the privy chamber in the 1560s.

Widowed by the first Earl of Essex in 1576, she married the Earl of Leicester in 1578 in a private ceremony conducted without the queen's knowledge, having been rumoured close to him for some years before. When Elizabeth learned of it she excluded Lettice from court permanently.

She was the mother of the second Earl of Essex and of Penelope Rich, the Stella of Sidney's sequence. She outlived Leicester, her son and the queen by many years, dying in 1634 at over ninety.

thomas_seymour.name: Thomas Seymour
thomas_seymour.desc:
Edward VI's younger uncle, created Baron Seymour of Sudeley and Lord Admiral, ambitious and resentful of the authority his elder brother had taken as Protector.

He married the widowed Catherine Parr in 1547, within months of Henry VIII's death and after having sought the hand of both Mary and Elizabeth. His conduct toward Elizabeth, then fourteen and living in the household, became the subject of a formal enquiry, and she was questioned closely about it.

He cultivated the young king with pocket money and worked to detach him from Somerset's control. Arrested in January 1549 after being found at night near the king's apartments, he was condemned by act of attainder rather than trial and executed in March.

francis_drake.name: Francis Drake
francis_drake.desc:
The first English commander to complete a circumnavigation of the globe, between 1577 and 1580, returning with plunder that repaid the investors many times over and earned him a knighthood aboard the Golden Hind at Deptford.

From a Plymouth family and a kinsman of Hawkins, he had sailed on the slaving voyage that ended in the Spanish attack at San Juan de Ulúa in 1568, and pursued Spain for the rest of his life. His raid on Cadiz in 1587 destroyed shipping and stores and delayed the Armada by a year.

He was vice-admiral in 1588 and helped choose the fireships sent in off Calais. The Lisbon expedition of 1589 failed expensively, and he died of dysentery off Panama in January 1596 on a last Caribbean voyage.

john_hawkins.name: John Hawkins
john_hawkins.desc:
Sea captain, shipowner and, from 1577, Treasurer of the Navy, who commanded the first English slaving voyages to West Africa and the Caribbean in the 1560s, trading in people taken by raid and purchase and selling them illegally into Spanish colonies.

The third voyage ended when Spanish forces attacked his ships at San Juan de Ulúa in 1568, an episode that shaped English attitudes to Spain for a generation. As Treasurer he directed the rebuilding of the fleet into lower, faster race-built galleons carrying heavier guns.

Those ships fought the Armada campaign, in which he commanded the Victory and was knighted at sea. He established the Chatham Chest, an early fund for disabled seamen, and died at sea off Puerto Rico in 1595.

martin_frobisher.name: Martin Frobisher
martin_frobisher.desc:
Commander of three voyages between 1576 and 1578 in search of a North-West Passage to Asia, reaching Baffin Island and returning with a black ore believed to contain gold.

Large sums were raised on the strength of it and a substantial mining operation mounted on the third voyage; the ore proved worthless and the Cathay Company collapsed, ruining several investors. Earlier and later he was employed in privateering and in service off the Irish coast.

He commanded the Triumph, the largest ship in the English fleet, against the Armada, holding the inshore station off Portland, and was knighted at sea during the campaign. He died in 1594 of a wound taken storming a fort at Crozon in Brittany.

richard_grenville.name: Richard Grenville
richard_grenville.desc:
A Cornish landowner, member of parliament and cousin of Raleigh, who had proposed a Pacific voyage in 1574 that the crown declined to authorise, the project passing afterwards to Drake.

He commanded the fleet that carried the first Roanoke colonists in 1585 and returned with supplies the following year, and was active in the plantation of Munster and in the defence of the West Country.

In 1591, off Flores in the Azores, the Revenge was cut off from Lord Thomas Howard's squadron by a much larger Spanish force. After an engagement lasting through the night the ship was taken and Grenville died of his wounds aboard a Spanish vessel; the Revenge was lost in a storm soon after.

charles_howard_effingham.name: Charles Howard of Effingham
charles_howard_effingham.desc:
Lord Admiral from 1585 and commander-in-chief of the English fleet against the Armada, later created Earl of Nottingham; a cousin of the queen through the Boleyn line.

He held supreme command in 1588 and took the principal decisions of the campaign: to engage from windward, to keep the range open rather than attempt boarding, and to send in fireships off Calais to break the Spanish formation. Holding together a fleet of independent and quarrelsome captains was among the harder parts of the task.

He defended Drake against accusations of deserting his station to take a prize, and spent his own money on relief for unpaid and diseased seamen when the crown did not. He commanded again at Cadiz in 1596 and lived to 1624.

humphrey_gilbert.name: Humphrey Gilbert
humphrey_gilbert.desc:
Half-brother of Raleigh, soldier in Ireland where he served with notorious severity, member of parliament, and author of a discourse arguing for a North-West Passage to Asia that circulated widely before publication in 1576.

He obtained letters patent in 1578 authorising him to discover and occupy lands not held by any Christian prince, the legal instrument on which the later Virginia charters were modelled, and made an unsuccessful first attempt that year.

In August 1583 he took formal possession of Newfoundland for the crown at St John's, the first English claim in North America. He was lost with the small frigate Squirrel on the return voyage, reportedly seen reading on deck shortly before she went down.

john_norreys.name: John Norreys
john_norreys.desc:
One of the most experienced English field commanders of the reign, who learned his trade in the Netherlands and served subsequently in Ireland, Portugal and Brittany.

He commanded English troops in Dutch service through the 1570s and 1580s, held the land forces during the Armada year, and led the Portugal expedition of 1589 with Drake, an expensive failure that damaged both reputations. In Brittany he fought the Catholic League with a small and chronically unpaid force.

He was closely associated with the development of a professional English infantry able to stand against Spanish formations, and with the officers who carried those methods into the next century. He died in Ireland in 1597.

francis_vere.name: Francis Vere
francis_vere.desc:
Commander of the English forces in Dutch service from 1589, and the most accomplished English soldier of the later reign, serving under Maurice of Nassau.

He fought at Nieuwpoort in 1600, where the English regiments held the dunes at heavy cost, and conducted the defence of Ostend through the first year of a siege that lasted three. His Commentaries, published after his death, are one of the earliest English professional accounts of war.

His campaigns kept the Dutch revolt alive and occupied a large part of Spain's army in the Netherlands, which was the strategic purpose of English intervention. He returned to England in 1604 and died in 1609.

thomas_cranmer.name: Thomas Cranmer
thomas_cranmer.desc:
Archbishop of Canterbury from 1533, a Cambridge scholar who came to the king's notice by suggesting that the universities of Europe rather than the pope should rule on the annulment.

He pronounced the first marriage void, and afterwards annulled the marriages to Anne Boleyn and Anne of Cleves. Under Edward VI he was able to legislate the doctrine he had held privately, producing the Books of Common Prayer of 1549 and 1552, the Ordinal and the Forty-Two Articles, and drawing continental theologians to England.

Deprived under Mary, tried for heresy and held at Oxford, he signed six recantations under pressure. At his execution in March 1556 he repudiated them and held his right hand in the fire. His liturgy remained the basis of English worship for four centuries.

reginald_pole.name: Reginald Pole
reginald_pole.desc:
A cousin of Henry VIII through his mother the Countess of Salisbury, and a Plantagenet by descent, educated at the king's expense in Padua among the leading humanists of Italy.

Asked for his opinion on the annulment, he answered with a sustained attack on the royal supremacy and left England for good. Made a cardinal in 1536, he was appointed legate to organise resistance; Henry could not reach him and executed his mother and brother instead. He came within a few votes of election as pope in 1549.

He returned in November 1554 as papal legate and absolved the realm of schism, becoming Archbishop of Canterbury after Cranmer's burning. His reforming synod planned seminaries that were never built. He died within hours of Mary in November 1558.

stephen_gardiner.name: Stephen Gardiner
stephen_gardiner.desc:
Bishop of Winchester from 1531, a canon lawyer who had worked on the annulment case in Rome and who defended the royal supremacy in print, while remaining firmly conservative on doctrine.

He opposed the evangelical direction of the later 1530s and 1540s, was outmanoeuvred by Cromwell and later by Cranmer, and spent the whole of Edward VI's reign in the Tower, refusing to accept the Prayer Book and being deprived of his see in 1551.

Released and restored by Mary in 1553, he became Lord Chancellor and drove the repeal of the Edwardian religious legislation and the restoration of the heresy laws. He negotiated the Spanish marriage treaty he privately disliked, and drew back from the burnings as their effect became clear. He died in November 1555.

hugh_latimer.name: Hugh Latimer
hugh_latimer.desc:
A prominent preacher of the English Reformation and Bishop of Worcester from 1535, whose plain, direct sermons attacked enclosure, rack-renting, corrupt judges and clerical wealth as vigorously as they attacked doctrine.

He resigned his see in 1539 over the conservative Act of Six Articles and was silenced and briefly imprisoned. Under Edward VI he preached regularly at court and at Paul's Cross, and his sermons before the young king are among the sharpest social criticism of the century.

Arrested under Mary, he was tried at Oxford with Ridley and Cranmer and burned in Broad Street on 16 October 1555, at about seventy. Foxe records his words to Ridley at the stake about lighting a candle in England that would never be put out.

nicholas_ridley.name: Nicholas Ridley
nicholas_ridley.desc:
Bishop of London under Edward VI and, with Cranmer, a principal architect of the reform of doctrine and worship in that reign, having moved from a Lutheran to a Reformed position on the eucharist.

He ordered the removal of stone altars in favour of communion tables, worked on the revision that produced the 1552 Prayer Book, and promoted the endowment of hospitals in London for the sick and poor.

He preached at Paul's Cross in July 1553 in support of Jane Grey's title, declaring both of Henry's daughters illegitimate, which left him no possible defence. Tried at Oxford and burned beside Latimer on 16 October 1555, his death was prolonged by badly built faggots, and Foxe's account of it circulated widely.

john_foxe.name: John Foxe
john_foxe.desc:
A fellow of Magdalen College who resigned over the statutes, tutor to the children of the executed Earl of Surrey, and a Protestant exile at Strasbourg, Frankfurt and Basel during Mary's reign.

There he began a Latin history of Christian persecution which he expanded, after returning in 1559, into Acts and Monuments, published in English in 1563. He gathered depositions, letters, court records and eyewitness accounts, and the work ran through four editions in his lifetime, each larger than the last.

He set the Marian burnings within a long history of the true church suffering under false authority, and argued for England as an elect nation. He opposed the death penalty for heresy even for Catholics, and pleaded unsuccessfully against the execution of Anabaptists in 1575.

matthew_parker.name: Matthew Parker
matthew_parker.desc:
Elizabeth I's first Archbishop of Canterbury, consecrated in 1559, a Cambridge scholar who had been chaplain to Anne Boleyn and who took the office reluctantly and only under pressure.

A moderate by temperament, he spent the archbishopric holding a middle line between returning exiles who wanted further reform and parishes reluctant to move at all. He oversaw the Thirty-Nine Articles and the Bishops' Bible, and issued the Advertisements on vestments in 1566 that provoked the first Puritan controversy.

He assembled a major collection of medieval English manuscripts dispersed by the dissolution, arguing that the early English church had been independent of Rome, and left it to Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, where much of it survives.

john_whitgift.name: John Whitgift
john_whitgift.desc:
Archbishop of Canterbury from 1583, a Cambridge administrator who had already fought the Puritan Thomas Cartwright in print over church government before he came to the see.

He required subscription to three articles affirming the royal supremacy, the Prayer Book and the Thirty-Nine Articles, and used the Court of High Commission and its ex officio oath to enforce them. Several hundred ministers were suspended, though many later conformed, and Burghley objected that the procedure resembled the Inquisition.

He had the queen's full support, and she is recorded as calling him her little black husband. He suppressed the Marprelate press, sat on the commission for Mary Stuart's trial, and attended Elizabeth at her death.

edmund_campion.name: Edmund Campion
edmund_campion.desc:
A noted Oxford scholar and orator who had taken deacon's orders in the English church, left for Douai and Rome, joined the Society of Jesus and taught in Prague before being sent on the English mission in 1580.

He travelled in disguise ministering to Catholic households and wrote the Decem Rationes, printed on a secret press and left in the university church at Oxford, offering to debate the Protestant divines. His Brag, circulated after capture, insisted that the mission was pastoral and would not touch matters of state.

Taken at Lyford Grange in July 1581 through an informer, he was held in the Tower, examined under torture three times, and brought out to public disputations without books or notes. He was executed at Tyburn on 1 December 1581 and canonised in 1970.

william_shakespeare.name: William Shakespeare
william_shakespeare.desc:
Actor, playwright and shareholder in the Lord Chamberlain's Men, from a Stratford glover's family, active in London from about 1592 and a housekeeper of the Globe from 1599.

His income came principally from his shares in the company and the playhouse rather than from writing. He wrote for a specific stage and a specific set of players: no scenery, daylight performance, an audience on three sides, and the same actors year after year, which is why the parts fit them so closely.

The narrative poems and the sonnets appeared in print in his lifetime; roughly half the plays did not, and eighteen survive only because Heminges and Condell collected them in the First Folio of 1623. He retired to Stratford and died in 1616.

christopher_marlowe.name: Christopher Marlowe
christopher_marlowe.desc:
Cambridge graduate, son of a Canterbury shoemaker, whose degree was granted in 1587 only after the Privy Council certified that he had been employed on the queen's service.

Tamburlaine established blank verse as the language of the popular stage, and The Jew of Malta, Edward II and Doctor Faustus followed within six years. His protagonists overreach deliberately and are destroyed by it, and the plays test orthodoxy hard enough that his own beliefs were repeatedly questioned.

He was arrested and released in 1593 while accusations of blasphemy circulated against him and Thomas Kyd was tortured over related papers. He was killed days later in a lodging house at Deptford, aged twenty-nine, in a dispute over a bill in the company of three men with government connections.

edmund_spenser.name: Edmund Spenser
edmund_spenser.desc:
Poet and colonial official, educated at Merchant Taylors' and Cambridge, who entered Leicester's household about 1579 and went to Ireland in 1580 as secretary to the Lord Deputy.

The Shepheardes Calender announced a deliberately archaic English and a Protestant pastoral politics. The Faerie Queene followed from his estate at Kilcolman in Munster, and Raleigh brought him to court to present it. He was granted a modest pension and no office in England.

His View of the Present State of Ireland argued for the destruction of Gaelic society by force and was not printed in his lifetime. Kilcolman was burned in Tyrone's rebellion in 1598 and he returned to London, dying there in January 1599.

ben_jonson.name: Ben Jonson
ben_jonson.desc:
Playwright, poet and critic, stepson of a bricklayer, who had soldiered in the Netherlands and killed a fellow actor in a duel, escaping the gallows by pleading benefit of clergy.

Every Man in His Humour was staged by the Chamberlain's Men in 1598 with Shakespeare in the cast. Volpone, The Alchemist and Bartholomew Fair followed, satirical comedies built on classical models and set in a closely observed London. He was imprisoned more than once over the political content of plays.

Under James he wrote the court masques, working with Inigo Jones until the two fell out over whether words or spectacle governed. His publication of his own plays as Works in 1616 made an unusual claim for the literary standing of drama.

john_lyly.name: John Lyly
john_lyly.desc:
Author of Euphues, the Anatomy of Wit and its sequel, whose ornate, antithetical and heavily figured prose was so widely imitated at court in the 1580s that the style acquired his character's name.

He wrote a series of comedies for the boys' companies, mostly mythological or pastoral in setting and performed before the queen, in which the plotting matters less than the patterned exchange of wit between characters.

That dialogue was a direct influence on later Elizabethan comedy, Shakespeare's included, both as a model and as something to parody. Lyly sat in four parliaments and petitioned unsuccessfully for years for the office of Master of the Revels, dying in relative obscurity in 1606.

richard_burbage.name: Richard Burbage
richard_burbage.desc:
The leading tragedian of the Lord Chamberlain's and later the King's Men, and the first player of Hamlet, Lear, Othello and Richard III, parts written with his particular range in mind.

His father James had built the Theatre in Shoreditch in 1576, the first purpose-built playhouse in England. When the lease on its ground failed, the company dismantled it over Christmas 1598 and carried the timbers across the Thames to build the Globe, which Richard and his brother Cuthbert half owned.

He was also a painter of some skill. At his death in 1619 the elegies listed the roles as though individual people had died with him, and Shakespeare had left him money for a memorial ring.

edward_alleyn.name: Edward Alleyn
edward_alleyn.desc:
A leading tragedian of the period, associated above all with Marlowe's principal roles — Tamburlaine, Barabas and Faustus — written for a voice that could carry an open yard.

He led the Admiral's Men, married Philip Henslowe's stepdaughter and became his partner in playhouses, property and the bear-baiting monopoly, and grew wealthy enough to retire from the stage in his thirties, returning briefly by royal request.

He bought the manor of Dulwich and founded the College of God's Gift there in 1619 as a school and almshouse, endowing it with his estate. The college's archive preserves Henslowe's papers, which is why so much is known about the business of Elizabethan theatre.

philip_henslowe.name: Philip Henslowe
philip_henslowe.desc:
Theatre owner, dyer, pawnbroker, property speculator and Groom of the Chamber, who built the Rose on Bankside in 1587 and later the Fortune and the Hope.

He financed the Admiral's Men, advanced money to dramatists against unfinished plays, bought costumes and properties, and stood surety for players in trouble. His relationship with the companies was that of a landlord and creditor rather than a member, which shaped the terms they worked on.

The diary and papers preserved at Dulwich record payments to writers, receipts by performance, inventories of costumes and stage properties, and the collaborative piecework by which most plays were actually written. They are the fullest surviving account of how the business operated.

thomas_wyatt.name: Thomas Wyatt
thomas_wyatt.desc:
Courtier and diplomat who served Henry VIII as ambassador to the emperor, and among the first to adapt the Italian sonnet and terza rima into English, working from Petrarch but sharpening the tone considerably.

None of his poems was printed in his lifetime; they circulated in manuscript at court and appeared in Tottel's Miscellany fifteen years after his death, where the editor smoothed his deliberately rough metre.

He was imprisoned in the Tower in 1536, when his earlier association with Anne Boleyn made him dangerous, and again in 1541 after Cromwell's fall, being pardoned on condition of returning to his wife. The poems that survive turn repeatedly on favour withdrawn and the hazard of standing close to power.

william_byrd.name: William Byrd
william_byrd.desc:
A leading composer of the period and a Gentleman of the Chapel Royal, a pupil of Thomas Tallis with whom he was granted a joint royal patent for printing music in 1575.

He wrote services and anthems for the Anglican rite, consort songs, and a large body of keyboard music that effectively founded the English virginalist school. He also composed three Latin masses and the Gradualia, published discreetly for the private use of recusant households.

He remained a practising Catholic throughout, was repeatedly presented as a recusant in the 1580s and 1590s, and lived latterly at Stondon Massey near the Petre family, who sheltered such worship. His position at court was never withdrawn.

john_dee.name: John Dee
john_dee.desc:
Mathematician, astrologer, antiquary and adviser on navigation, who assembled at Mortlake the largest private library in England, some four thousand volumes, open to scholars.

He instructed English pilots in the mathematics of navigation, advised on the search for a North-East and North-West Passage, selected an auspicious date for Elizabeth's coronation, and argued in his Brytanici Imperii Limites for an English title to territory in the north Atlantic based on prior discovery. The phrase British Empire is generally credited to him.

From 1582 he worked with the scryer Edward Kelley in extended attempts at communication with angels, travelling with him through central Europe. He returned to find his library plundered and died in poverty about 1609.

thomas_gresham.name: Thomas Gresham
thomas_gresham.desc:
Crown financial agent in Antwerp under four monarchs, who raised and refinanced royal loans on the exchange there and reported continuously to the government on credit, bullion and Netherlandish politics.

He advised on the recoinage of 1560 that withdrew the debased money of the previous two reigns, and argued consistently for reducing the crown's dependence on foreign lenders in favour of borrowing at home from the City. The principle later named Gresham's Law was not his formulation, though it carries his name.

He built the Royal Exchange in London in 1571 at his own expense, modelled on the Antwerp bourse, and left his estate to found Gresham College, where free public lectures began in 1597.

nicholas_hilliard.name: Nicholas Hilliard
nicholas_hilliard.desc:
Goldsmith and limner to Elizabeth I, and the leading English painter of portrait miniatures, trained in the goldsmith's trade and working in watercolour on vellum laid on card.

He painted the queen without shadow at her own direction, producing the flat, radiant and unaging image that became the official face of the reign, and portrayed most of the court besides. The Young Man Among Roses is generally taken as the outstanding surviving example of the emblematic miniature.

His treatise, The Arte of Limning, is the earliest English writing on the practice of painting. Despite constant employment he was chronically short of money and was briefly imprisoned for debt.

richard_hakluyt.name: Richard Hakluyt
richard_hakluyt.desc:
Clergyman and geographer, educated at Westminster and Christ Church, who devoted his career to collecting and editing the accounts of English voyages and to arguing for overseas expansion.

He served as chaplain to the English embassy in Paris, where the evidence of French and Spanish activity sharpened his case. His Discourse of Western Planting, written for Raleigh in 1584 and presented to the queen, argued for colonies in North America on grounds of trade, employment, naval strength and the containment of Spain.

The Principal Navigations, published from 1589 and expanded to three volumes, gathered narratives, logs, letters and patents. He was a founding adventurer of the Virginia Company, and the record he assembled shaped English colonial argument for a century.

roger_ascham.name: Roger Ascham
roger_ascham.desc:
Humanist scholar of St John's College, Cambridge, and a noted Greek scholar, who tutored the young Elizabeth in Greek and Latin and served as Latin secretary to Edward VI, Mary I and Elizabeth in turn, keeping the post under Mary without changing his religion.

Toxophilus, a dialogue on archery published in 1545, was written deliberately in English to show the language fit for serious argument. The Scholemaster, published after his death, advocated teaching by double translation, patience and encouragement rather than the beatings then usual in grammar schools.

He boasted of Elizabeth's fluency, and her habit of answering ambassadors in Latin without preparation dates from those lessons. He died in 1568 leaving little money.

hans_holbein.name: Hans Holbein the Younger
hans_holbein.desc:
Painter from Augsburg, established at Basel, who came to England in 1526 with a recommendation from Erasmus to Thomas More and returned in 1532 to work for the merchants of the Steelyard and then the court.

Court painter from 1536, he produced the Whitehall mural of Henry VII, Elizabeth of York, Henry VIII and Jane Seymour, whose frontal stance fixed the standard image of the king. The palace burned in 1698 and the composition is known through a surviving cartoon and copies.

He drew a large part of the court in coloured chalks, a body of work now at Windsor that is the closest thing to a photographic record of the period. Sent abroad to portray prospective brides, he painted Anne of Cleves in 1539 and died in London of plague in 1543.

philip_ii.name: Philip II of Spain
philip_ii.desc:
King of Spain from 1556, ruler also of the Netherlands, Naples, Milan and the Indies, and from 1580 of Portugal; king consort of England during his marriage to Mary I, in which the treaty gave him the title and almost no power.

He governed through paper, reading and annotating dispatches personally from the Escorial, and his revenues from American silver were repeatedly outrun by the cost of the Netherlands revolt and three state bankruptcies.

He authorised the Armada of 1588 to end English intervention in the Netherlands and restore Catholicism, planning the campaign in detail from Madrid and insisting on a junction with Parma for which no deep-water port had been secured. He continued the war with England until his death in 1598.

charles_v.name: Charles V
charles_v.desc:
Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain, ruler of the Burgundian Netherlands and the American possessions, and nephew of Catherine of Aragon through his mother Joanna of Castile.

His troops sacked Rome in 1527 and left Clement VII effectively under his control, which is the principal reason the annulment case was never determined in Henry's favour. He treated his aunt's cause as both a family obligation and a point of diplomatic leverage over England.

He spent his reign at war with France and with the Lutheran princes, conceding the Peace of Augsburg in 1555, and then divided his inheritance, leaving Spain and the Netherlands to Philip II and the imperial title to his brother Ferdinand before retiring to a monastery in 1556.

clement_vii.name: Pope Clement VII
clement_vii.desc:
Pope from 1523, a Medici and a cautious politician, whose pontificate was dominated by the rivalry between Charles V and Francis I and by the consequences of choosing the losing side.

After the sack of Rome in 1527 he was besieged in the Castel Sant'Angelo and afterwards operated under imperial constraint. He could not annul the marriage of the emperor's aunt whatever the canonical merits, so he deferred: granting a legatine commission, then revoking the case to Rome in 1529.

He gave sentence for Catherine in March 1534, by which time England had already legislated away papal jurisdiction. He died later that year, having also failed to settle the German question.

pius_v.name: Pope Pius V
pius_v.desc:
Pope from 1566, formerly a Dominican inquisitor, austere in personal life and rigorous in enforcing the decrees of the Council of Trent, and later canonised.

He issued the bull Regnans in Excelsis in February 1570, excommunicating Elizabeth I, declaring her deposed and purporting to release her subjects from allegiance. He acted without consulting Philip II or the emperor, both of whom thought it reckless, and it arrived too late to assist the Northern Rising it was meant to support.

Its practical effect in England was to place Catholics under suspicion of disloyalty and to supply the justification for the penal legislation that followed. He also organised the league that defeated the Ottoman fleet at Lepanto in 1571.

duke_of_parma.name: Alexander Farnese, Duke of Parma
duke_of_parma.desc:
Alexander Farnese, nephew of Philip II, governor-general of the Netherlands from 1578 and widely regarded by contemporaries as the ablest soldier of his generation in Europe.

He recovered the southern provinces for Spain by a combination of siege warfare and skilful political concession to Catholic nobles, taking Antwerp in 1585 after a fourteen-month siege in which he bridged the Scheldt. That success was what prompted English intervention on the Dutch side.

In 1588 his army of some 27,000 waited at Dunkirk and Nieuwpoort to be escorted across by the Armada, but no deep-water port was in Spanish hands and Dutch flyboats blockaded the shallows. The junction was never made. He was afterwards diverted into France against Henry of Navarre and died in 1592.

medina_sidonia.name: Duke of Medina Sidonia
medina_sidonia.desc:
A Spanish grandee of great wealth and administrative competence, appointed to command the Armada in 1588 after the death of the Marquis of Santa Cruz.

He wrote to Philip on appointment that he had no experience of naval war, was habitually seasick, and lacked the health and the means for the task, and asked to be excused; the king refused and the letter was intercepted by his secretaries. He had in fact organised much of the fleet's supply.

He held the formation through the Channel engagements with considerable discipline, but the plan gave him no way of embarking Parma's army, and after the fireships off Calais and the action at Gravelines he took the fleet north around Scotland. Roughly half of it returned.

bosworth.name: Battle of Bosworth
bosworth.desc:
The battle fought on 22 August 1485 in Leicestershire, at which Richard III was killed and Henry Tudor took the crown, ending the main phase of the Wars of the Roses.

Henry had landed at Milford Haven with a small force of French, Scottish and Welsh troops and gathered support crossing Wales. He was outnumbered on the day, and the outcome turned on the Stanleys, who brought several thousand men to the field and withheld them until Richard committed to a charge at Henry's person.

Richard was the last English king to die in battle. Chroniclers record the crown being recovered from the field and set on Henry's head. The site was securely identified only in recent decades, and Richard's remains were found in Leicester in 2012.

field_cloth_gold.name: Field of the Cloth of Gold
field_cloth_gold.desc:
The meeting of Henry VIII and Francis I in the Val d'Or near Guînes in June 1520, arranged by Wolsey as a demonstration of English importance in the balance between France and the Empire.

It lasted some seventeen days and involved perhaps six thousand people, housed in tents and in a temporary palace of timber, canvas and glass erected outside Guînes, with fountains running wine and a programme of tournaments in which both kings took part.

Chroniclers report a wrestling bout between the two, though the accounts are late and unreliable. The expense was enormous and fell on both crowns and their nobilities. Henry met Charles V immediately before and after, and within two years England was at war with France.

dissolution.name: Dissolution of the Monasteries
dissolution.desc:
The suppression of England's monasteries, priories, friaries and convents between 1536 and 1540, and the transfer of their property to the crown.

It proceeded in stages: a valuation of ecclesiastical wealth in 1535, visitations producing evidence of laxity, an act suppressing the smaller houses in 1536, and then the taking of surrenders from the greater ones. Around eight hundred houses were dissolved and some ten thousand religious pensioned off or turned out.

Most of the land was sold within a decade to pay for war rather than retained, so the crown's long-term gain was limited while the gentry and merchants who bought it acquired a permanent interest in the settlement. It was the largest transfer of property in English history, and it removed the principal provider of charity and hospitality.

pilgrimage_grace.name: Pilgrimage of Grace
pilgrimage_grace.desc:
A large rising across Yorkshire, Lincolnshire and the north in the autumn of 1536, provoked by the dissolution of the smaller monasteries, taxation, and hostility to Cromwell and the reforming bishops.

The rebels numbered perhaps thirty thousand, far more than the force Norfolk could put in the field, and marched under a banner of the Five Wounds of Christ describing themselves as pilgrims rather than rebels. Their articles demanded the restoration of the abbeys, the removal of the king's advisers, and a parliament at York.

Norfolk negotiated, offering a pardon and a parliament he had no authority to grant. The host dispersed on that promise. When fresh disturbances broke out in 1537 the crown treated the pardon as void, and the leaders, including Robert Aske, were tried and executed.

wyatt_rebellion.name: Wyatt's Rebellion
wyatt_rebellion.desc:
A rising in Kent in January and February 1554, led by Thomas Wyatt the Younger, son of the poet, against Mary I's proposed marriage to Philip of Spain.

It was one part of a wider plan for simultaneous risings in the Midlands, the West Country and the Welsh Marches, all of which failed to materialise. Wyatt raised some three thousand men, secured Rochester, and marched on London, where the bridge was held against him and his force crossed at Kingston.

Mary refused to leave the city and made a direct appeal at the Guildhall, and London did not rise. The rebels were halted at Ludgate and surrendered. The failure cost Jane Grey and her husband their lives and sent Elizabeth to the Tower on suspicion of complicity that was never proved.

marian_persecution.name: The Marian Burnings
marian_persecution.desc:
The prosecution of Protestants for heresy under the revived medieval statutes between February 1555 and November 1558, in which around 280 people were burned, most of them in London, Kent, Essex and Sussex.

The victims included bishops — Cranmer, Ridley, Latimer, Hooper, Ferrar — but the great majority were artisans, labourers and their wives, tried in diocesan courts and executed locally so that neighbours would see it. About fifty were women.

The policy did not suppress Protestant belief, and Gardiner and others drew back as it became clear that the executions were producing sympathy rather than conformity. John Foxe recorded them in detail from depositions and eyewitness accounts, and his book fixed the reign's reputation for the following three centuries.

babington_plot.name: Babington Plot
babington_plot.desc:
A conspiracy of 1586 by Anthony Babington and a group of young Catholic gentlemen to assassinate Elizabeth I, free Mary, Queen of Scots and place her on the throne with Spanish support.

Walsingham's service controlled it from the outset. Mary's correspondence had been cut off, and Gilbert Gifford was placed to offer her a channel by which letters passed in and out of Chartley in a waterproof case through the bung of a beer barrel, every one of them copied and deciphered by Thomas Phelippes before delivery.

Mary's written reply approving the design was the evidence required, and a forged postscript was added asking for the conspirators' names. Babington and thirteen others were executed in September 1586, and Mary was tried at Fotheringhay the following month.

spanish_armada.name: The Spanish Armada
spanish_armada.desc:
The Spanish invasion fleet of 1588: some 130 ships carrying around 19,000 soldiers, ordered to sail up the Channel, meet Parma's army off Flanders and escort it across to England.

The English engaged from windward at long range through nine days of running fight, doing limited damage but preventing the boarding actions the Spanish tactics required. Fireships sent in off Calais on the night of 7 August broke the crescent formation, and the action at Gravelines the next day did the real damage.

With the wind against a return down the Channel, the fleet went north around Scotland and Ireland, where storms and a coast without charts destroyed a large part of it. The campaign did not end the war, which ran another fifteen years, but its outcome was widely read in England as providential.

essex_rebellion.name: Essex's Rebellion
essex_rebellion.desc:
The Earl of Essex's attempt on 8 February 1601 to raise the City of London, seize the court and remove the Cecil interest from the queen's counsels.

He had returned from Ireland without leave in 1599, been confined, tried before a commission and stripped of the sweet wines monopoly on which his finances depended. His house became a gathering point for the disaffected, and rumours that Cecil favoured a Spanish claimant were used to justify what followed.

Some two hundred men went into the City with him. No one joined, the proclamation of him as a traitor was read, and he was back at Essex House by afternoon and surrendered that night. He was tried with the Earl of Southampton and executed at the Tower on 25 February.

tower_of_london.name: Tower of London
tower_of_london.desc:
A royal fortress begun by William the Conqueror on the Thames, serving in the Tudor period as armoury, treasury, mint, royal menagerie, lodging before coronation and the principal state prison.

Prisoners of rank were kept in the Bell, Beauchamp and Salt Towers and in the lieutenant's lodgings rather than in dungeons, at their own expense, with servants and books; the graffiti they cut into the stone survives. Torture required a warrant from the Council and was used chiefly on suspected priests and conspirators.

Anne Boleyn, Catherine Howard and Jane Grey were executed on the green within the walls; most others died on Tower Hill outside. Elizabeth herself was held there for two months in 1554 and rode through it in state before her coronation four years later.

hampton_court.name: Hampton Court Palace
hampton_court.desc:
A palace on the Thames west of London, leased by Wolsey in 1514 and rebuilt by him on a scale no subject could safely afford, with lodgings for a household of several hundred and for visiting royalty.

He transferred it to Henry VIII in 1529 as his position failed. Henry doubled it, adding the great hall with its hammerbeam roof, the kitchens, the tennis court and the astronomical clock, and installing a water supply piped three miles from Coombe Hill.

Edward VI was born there in October 1537 and Jane Seymour died there twelve days later. Elizabeth used it regularly, and the Hampton Court Conference on the future of the church was held there under James I in 1604.

the_globe.name: The Globe
the_globe.desc:
The Bankside playhouse opened in 1599, built from the timbers of the Theatre in Shoreditch, which the Lord Chamberlain's Men dismantled over Christmas 1598 when the lease on its ground failed and carried across the river.

It was polygonal, open to the sky over the yard, holding perhaps three thousand people standing and seated in three galleries, with performances by daylight in the afternoon. There was no scenery to speak of; place was established in the words and by properties carried on.

Unusually, it was owned by the players themselves — the Burbages held half and five sharers including Shakespeare the rest — so the leading actors had a direct interest in the receipts. It burned down in 1613 when a cannon fired during Henry VIII ignited the thatch.

tilbury.name: Tilbury Camp
tilbury.desc:
The camp in Essex where the land army assembled in August 1588 against the threat of invasion, sited to cover the approach to London where a boom had been thrown across the Thames.

The troops were largely untrained county levies, gathered slowly and badly supplied, and the force would have faced Parma's veterans had they landed. Leicester organised the camp and arranged the queen's visit to it.

Elizabeth reviewed the troops on 9 August, by which date the Armada had already been driven past the Straits and was making north, though this was not yet known at Tilbury. The speech recorded as referring to the heart and stomach of a king survives only in later copies, and its exact wording is uncertain.

fotheringhay.name: Fotheringhay Castle
fotheringhay.desc:
A castle in Northamptonshire, a Yorkist property and the birthplace of Richard III, chosen in 1586 as the place to try Mary, Queen of Scots because it was secure, remote and defensible.

She was moved there in September, and tried in the great hall in October before a commission of some thirty-six peers, privy councillors and judges. She was allowed no counsel and not shown the letters used against her, and refused to recognise the court's jurisdiction over an anointed and foreign queen before eventually answering.

She was executed in the hall on 8 February 1587. The castle was neglected afterwards and had largely gone by the seventeenth century; only earthworks and a fragment of masonry remain.

hardwick_hall.name: Hardwick Hall
hardwick_hall.desc:
A house in Derbyshire built for Bess of Hardwick between 1590 and 1597, next to the older hall in which she had been born, to designs associated with Robert Smythson.

It is compact, tall and almost symmetrical, with the state rooms placed on the top floor rather than the ground, and windows increasing in size with each storey — the source of the rhyme about more glass than wall. Her initials stand in openwork stone along the roofline.

The long gallery, the plaster frieze in the High Great Chamber and a substantial collection of sixteenth-century textiles survive largely intact, because the family later preferred Chatsworth and left it alone. It is among the best-preserved examples of the Elizabethan prodigy house.

act_of_supremacy.name: Act of Supremacy (1534)
act_of_supremacy.desc:
The statute of 1534 declaring that the king was and had always been Supreme Head of the Church of England, framed as recognition of an existing right rather than as an innovation.

It followed the Act in Restraint of Appeals of 1533, which had asserted that England was an empire whose crown answered to no external jurisdiction, and it was accompanied by a Treasons Act making it capital to deny the title in words. That provision is what brought More and Bishop Fisher to trial.

The supremacy placed the church settlement in the hands of king and parliament, so that doctrine and worship could be remade by statute — as they duly were, in different directions, in 1549, 1553 and 1559. It was repealed under Mary and re-enacted in modified form for Elizabeth.

book_of_common_prayer.name: Book of Common Prayer
book_of_common_prayer.desc:
The English liturgy compiled largely by Cranmer, issued in 1549 and revised in a more clearly reformed direction in 1552, drawing on the Sarum use, Lutheran orders and patristic sources.

The 1549 book replaced the Latin rite with a single vernacular volume covering the whole year and every occasion, and was conservative enough in wording to be read in a traditional sense, which is what provoked the Prayer Book rebellion in Cornwall and Devon. The 1552 revision removed that ambiguity, stripping the eucharistic language of any suggestion of sacrifice.

Elizabeth's book of 1559 restored some of the earlier phrasing deliberately, so that most consciences could conform. Its collects and cadences had a lasting influence on English prose.

act_of_uniformity.name: Act of Uniformity (1559)
act_of_uniformity.desc:
The statute of 1559 requiring the use of a revised Book of Common Prayer in every parish, with penalties for clergy who refused and for parishioners who stayed away from church.

It passed the Lords by three votes, with two Marian bishops in prison and the rest opposing, and was managed through by Cecil. The book restored the 1552 text with changes calculated to blunt its sharpest edges, notably combining the words of administration from both earlier books so that communicants might understand them as they chose.

With the accompanying Act of Supremacy, which made the queen Supreme Governor rather than Supreme Head, it established a church reformed in doctrine and episcopal in structure. Whitgift's subscription campaign of the 1580s was an attempt to enforce it fully.

book_of_martyrs.name: Foxe's Book of Martyrs
book_of_martyrs.desc:
John Foxe's Acts and Monuments, a long history of the Church presented as a struggle between the true faith and a corrupted authority, concentrating on the sufferings of those who resisted.

First published in English in 1563 and expanded through three further editions in Foxe's lifetime, it ran to several million words and was illustrated with woodcuts of the executions. Foxe worked from depositions, letters, official records and eyewitnesses, and his documentation is better than his reputation for credulity suggests.

Convocation ordered copies placed in cathedral churches and the houses of senior clergy, giving it a semi-official standing, and it was among the most widely read books of the period. It shaped English attitudes to Catholicism, and to England's place in providential history, for centuries.

faerie_queene.name: The Faerie Queene
faerie_queene.desc:
Spenser's allegorical epic, published in three books in 1590 and six in 1596, in which knights representing the moral virtues undertake quests in the service of Gloriana, the Faerie Queene.

It was planned in twelve books and left unfinished, with the fragmentary Mutability Cantos appearing after his death. Spenser devised a nine-line stanza for it, closing with an alexandrine, and wrote in a deliberately archaic vocabulary intended to give English a literary past comparable to Italy's.

It works simultaneously as chivalric romance, moral allegory, Protestant polemic and sustained compliment to Elizabeth, who appears refracted as both Gloriana and Belphoebe. Contemporary politics run beneath the surface throughout, including the Netherlands, Mary Stuart's trial and Ireland.

hamlet.name: Hamlet
hamlet.desc:
Shakespeare's tragedy of about 1600, written for Burbage and the Globe and drawing on an earlier revenge play, now lost, that had been on the London stage for a decade.

It takes the conventions of the revenge tragedy — a ghost, a duty of vengeance, a feigned madness, a final bloodbath — and interrupts them repeatedly with a protagonist who reflects instead of acting, which is what gave the English stage a new kind of interior life.

It survives in three markedly different early texts: a short quarto of 1603, a much longer one of 1604, and the Folio of 1623, which cuts some passages and adds others. No modern edition is simply the play as first performed, and editors must choose.

doctor_faustus.name: Doctor Faustus
doctor_faustus.desc:
Marlowe's tragedy of a scholar who contracts with the devil for twenty-four years of knowledge and power, based on the German Faustbuch and written for Edward Alleyn.

It stages damnation without mitigating it: the bargain is real, the theology is orthodox, and the last soliloquy plays out an hour that cannot be stopped. Comic scenes of conjuring, some probably by other hands, sit alongside that and were expanded in performance.

It survives in two substantially different versions, the shorter published in 1604 and a longer one in 1616 with additional material paid for by Henslowe. It was among the most frequently performed plays of the period, and contemporary anecdotes about real devils appearing on stage indicate the effect it had.

regnans_in_excelsis.name: Regnans in Excelsis
regnans_in_excelsis.desc:
The papal bull issued by Pius V in February 1570, excommunicating Elizabeth I, declaring her deposed as a pretended queen and servant of crime, and purporting to absolve her subjects from all obedience to her.

It was issued without consultation with Philip II or the emperor, both of whom regarded it as damaging, and arrived after the Northern Rising it might have supported had already collapsed. A copy was nailed to the Bishop of London's gate by John Felton, who was executed for it.

Its effect in England was to make loyalty and religion formally incompatible for Catholics and to justify the treason legislation of 1571 and after. Later missionary priests were routinely pressed at trial to say whether Elizabeth was lawfully queen, a question the bull had made unanswerable.

links.details: Anne's daughter arrived instead of the son that would have justified everything. Elizabeth rarely mentioned her mother, but she wore Anne's initial ring and promoted her Boleyn relatives throughout the reign.
She entered by the royal apartments where she had lodged before her coronation, and was executed on the green within the walls. Her body was buried in the chapel of St Peter ad Vincula.
