Anne kept the standing of the King's Sister after the annulment and returned to the palace as an honoured guest, dining with the daughters of the man who had divorced her.

They were married in November 1501 and sent to Ludlow; Arthur was dead by April. Catherine swore for the rest of her life that the marriage was never consummated, which was the whole legal ground on which her second marriage stood.

Both were fifteen. The five months at Ludlow left no witness able to settle the question either way, and thirty years later the depositions taken on it were the recollections of elderly servants about what had been said at the time.
Burbage acted in Jonson's early comedies, and Jonson wrote parts that demanded exactly the range Burbage had built on Shakespeare's tragedies.
Jonson wrote for the Chamberlain's Men, who staged Every Man in His Humour with Shakespeare in the cast, though he kept a critical distance from the popular playhouse.

Jonson thought Shakespeare careless and said he wished he had blotted a thousand lines. He also wrote the poem that calls him the soul of the age.

The memorial poem for the First Folio calls him not of an age but for all time; the Discoveries, published later, record the reservation about blotting lines and add that he loved the man on this side idolatry. Both judgements have been quoted ever since, usually separately.
Bess served in the privy chamber and stayed close enough to the queen to survive several spells of disgrace over her marriages and her granddaughter's royal blood.

Widowed for the fourth time and in possession of a large income, Bess rebuilt the house of her birth between 1590 and 1597 to designs associated with Robert Smythson. Her initials stand in openwork stone along the roofline.
Burghley was Bess's correspondent through the years when her husband was Mary Stuart's keeper, and she wrote to him about both the security of the prisoner and the wreck of her marriage.

She was held first at Syon and brought to the Tower in February 1542. Foxe and later chroniclers record that she asked for the block to be brought to her room the night before, though the account is not contemporary.

Mary was the only one of Catherine's children to survive infancy, and mother and daughter were kept apart for the last years of Catherine's life. Mary's Catholicism and her loyalty to Spain both came from this.

Parr brought Elizabeth into her household after 1543 and secured her instruction under reformist scholars including John Cheke and Roger Ascham.

Her own published devotions and her regency in 1544 gave Elizabeth a working precedent for a learned Protestant queen exercising authority.

Parr had wanted Seymour before Henry chose her, and married him within months of the king's death. The haste caused scandal and the marriage brought Elizabeth into a household that was not safe for her.
Suffolk ran the English jousts alongside the king, in the tiltyard where the two courts spent seventeen days proving they were not afraid of each other.

Brandon was the king's tilting partner and the only man at court who could tell him unwelcome things and survive. He married Henry's sister Mary in secret in 1515 and was fined rather than executed.

The fine for the marriage was set at £24,000, payable in instalments, and much of it was never collected. Brandon was the only one of Henry's early companions to die in his bed and at court, and the king paid for his funeral at Windsor.

Howard defended Drake against captains who accused him of deserting his station on the first night of the campaign to take the damaged Rosario as a prize. Holding a command of independent and quarrelsome captains together through nine days of running engagement was among his more difficult tasks.

Howard had a Lord Admiral's authority and a courtier's caution; Drake had the fighting reputation and no patience for command structures. The working arrangement between them held through the campaign, and Howard's willingness to take Drake's tactical advice while retaining the decision was much of why it worked.

Howard held supreme command as Lord Admiral and took the principal decisions of the campaign: to engage from windward, to keep the range open rather than attempt boarding, and to break the Spanish crescent formation with fireships off Calais on the night of 7 August.

He afterwards spent his own money on relief for unpaid and sick seamen when the crown did not.

Catherine was Charles's maternal aunt, and he treated the annulment proceedings as both a family matter and a point of diplomatic leverage. Imperial influence over Rome after 1527 is the principal reason the case was never determined in Henry's favour.

He never met the political cost of defending her, since imperial interests in Italy required a compliant pope in any case, and the two objectives coincided. Catherine's appeals to him were answered with diplomatic pressure rather than the military threat she occasionally hoped for.

Imperial troops sacked Rome in 1527 and held the pope effectively prisoner. From that point Clement could not rule against the emperor's aunt whatever the merits of Henry's case.

The imperial army that took Rome in May 1527 was largely unpaid and beyond its commanders' control, and the sack lasted eight days. Clement was besieged in the Castel Sant'Angelo, capitulated after a month, and remained effectively a prisoner until he escaped in disguise that December.

They allied against France repeatedly and each abandoned the other when terms suited. Charles was Catherine's nephew, which made the alliance useless the moment the annulment began.

Henry declared war on France in 1512, 1522 and 1543 in concert with the emperor, and was left to make separate terms each time. The 1543 alliance produced the capture of Boulogne in 1544, held at great expense and sold back to France in 1550.

Philip was raised to inherit Spain, the Netherlands and the Indies while his father held the empire together by travelling it. The abdication of 1555 handed him a Habsburg quarrel with England that he then married into.

Charles wrote his son a private political testament in 1548 advising him to trust no minister completely and to keep the Netherlands at all costs, advice Philip followed to the point of repeated state bankruptcies brought on by the revolt.
Hatton was mocked as the dancing chancellor, but he managed the Commons for the crown, sat on the commission that tried Mary Stuart, and died owing the queen a fortune she had lent him.
Hatton was among the principal investors in the circumnavigation. Drake renamed his ship the Golden Hind during the voyage, adopting the hind that appeared in Hatton's coat of arms.
Two favourites competing for the same attention, they quarrelled over precedence and patronage while cooperating on the Privy Council against Spain.

Marlowe took a German legend and made the damnation literal and the theology inescapable. Comic scenes were added later by other hands, and the play survives in two versions twelve years apart.

The A-text of 1604 and the B-text of 1616 differ by some six hundred lines, with Henslowe recording a payment to Birde and Rowley in 1602 for additions. Which version represents Marlowe's play is unresolved and probably unresolvable.

Alleyn created Tamburlaine, Barabas and Faustus, and Marlowe wrote those parts for a voice that could fill an open yard.

Alleyn was about twenty-one when he first played Tamburlaine, and the parts written for him are all men who talk their way to power and are destroyed by the same appetite. He kept the Marlowe repertory for the Admiral's Men after the playwright's death.

Marlowe established blank verse, the overreaching protagonist and the English history play on the commercial stage, and Shakespeare's early work responds directly to those models.

After Marlowe's death in 1593 Shakespeare quoted a line of his in As You Like It, one of the few explicit acknowledgements of one dramatist by another in the period.

Clement spent six years avoiding a decision on the annulment because the emperor's army controlled Rome. The final sentence for Catherine in 1534 came long after England had already legislated itself out of his jurisdiction.
Parma's tercios and Vere's English regiments fought over the same Dutch river towns for a decade, in the sieges that turned English soldiering professional.

Parma had assembled an army and a fleet of barges at Dunkirk and Nieuwpoort, but no deep-water port was in Spanish hands and Dutch flyboats blockaded the shallows. He received no adequate warning of the fleet's arrival, and the two forces never joined.

He had told Philip in 1586 that the crossing needed either surprise or a deep-water port, and that a fleet from Spain would supply neither. His army waited in the barges for a fortnight in conditions that produced serious sickness before he stood it down.
The bull was the reason missionary priests could be treated as agents of a foreign power. Campion was pressed at his trial to say whether the queen was lawfully queen, which was the whole trap.

Campion was held in the Tower from July 1581 and examined under torture on three occasions. He was brought out to take part in public disputations with Protestant divines, conducted without access to books or notes.

He was offered his life and preferment if he would conform, and the disputations were arranged partly to demonstrate that he could be beaten in argument. Observers reported that he held his own, and no further sessions were held.
Spenser held colonial office in Munster for nearly twenty years and wrote a hard-line tract on governing Ireland. The queen granted him a pension for the poem and little else.

Spenser planned twelve books, each treating a virtue through the adventures of a knight, and completed six along with the fragmentary Mutability Cantos.

For it he devised a nine-line stanza and a deliberately archaic vocabulary, and framed the whole as a compliment to Elizabeth in the figures of Gloriana and Belphoebe.

Alleyn's Faustus was famous enough that stories circulated of a real devil appearing on stage during a performance.

He is described as playing the part in a surplice with a cross stitched on it. The story of a devil appearing among the actors at Exeter, which sent the company out of town, was in circulation within a generation and says more about the play's effect than its staging.
Alleyn married Henslowe's stepdaughter and became his partner in playhouses, bear gardens and property. Between them they controlled the Rose, the Fortune and the Admiral's Men.
As uncle to the king he took the title of Protector and ruled almost as a monarch, pushing reform faster than the country would take.

Dudley led the coup that removed Somerset from the Protectorate in 1549 and, after a brief reconciliation, had him executed in 1552.

Somerset's fall in 1549 was engineered by a coalition of conservatives and reformers that Dudley then broke, discarding the conservatives once he was in power. The second charge against Somerset in 1551 was of plotting a banquet at which his rivals would be seized.

The Prayer Books were imposed by Acts of Uniformity in 1549 and 1552, the first provoking rebellion in Cornwall and Devon by men who called it a Christmas game.

The Western rebels demanded the restoration of the Latin mass and the Act of Six Articles, and Cranmer's reply to them survives. Around 4,000 people died in the suppression, more than in any other rising of the century.

The two youngest children were brought up together under reformist tutors and wrote to each other in Latin. Edward's Protestant education is much of the reason Elizabeth's settlement went the way it did.

Elizabeth cultivated the contrast with Mary in these years, appearing plainly dressed and studious. Their correspondence stopped when Thomas Seymour's fall made contact dangerous.

Dying at fifteen, Edward drew up a Device for the Succession excluding both his half-sisters and settling the crown on his Protestant cousin. It had no statutory force, and lasted nine days.

The Device was drafted by the dying king in his own hand and altered from heirs male to Jane and her heirs male as it became clear he had no time. Judges signed it under protest and only after a pardon under the great seal.

Edward's council pressed Mary to give up the Mass, and she refused with imperial backing. The quarrel over her household chapel was the sharpest religious confrontation of his reign.

Mary's household mass, attended by hundreds, was defended by imperial threat of war and by her flat refusal to obey. The confrontation ended with Edward in tears and the Council conceding in practice while denying it in principle.

The settlement of 1559 passed the Lords by three votes with two bishops in prison. It imposed a Prayer Book deliberately ambiguous on the eucharist, so that most consciences could just about accept it.

The words of administration combined the 1549 and 1552 formulas, so that a communicant could understand the sacrament as presence or as memorial. The Ornaments Rubric preserved traditional vestments on paper, which supplied the ground for a century of subsequent quarrels.

Campion maintained that his mission was pastoral and not political, and was convicted of conspiring against the queen on evidence that historians generally regard as unfounded. He was executed at Tyburn on 1 December 1581 under the penalty for treason.

He was tried with others under a statute of Edward III on an alleged conspiracy in Rome and Reims, because the government preferred a treason charge to a heresy one. He was drawn on a hurdle to Tyburn in the rain and hanged, drawn and quartered with two companions.

The queen invested in the circumnavigation and received a large share of the proceeds, while publicly disclaiming responsibility to the Spanish ambassador. She knighted Drake aboard the Golden Hind at Deptford in April 1581.

The queen's investment was concealed and her share of the treasure — variously estimated but very large — went into the exchequer and helped fund the Netherlands intervention. She had the ceremonial sword handed to the French ambassador to perform the knighting, so that France was implicated too.

Gilbert held letters patent from the queen to discover and occupy lands not held by any Christian prince, the legal basis of the later Virginia charters.

The patent gave him six years to plant a colony, with title to the land and jurisdiction over the settlers, and reserved a fifth of any gold to the crown. It was reissued to Raleigh after Gilbert's death and became the template for the Virginia charters of 1606.

Elizabeth refused all her life to name a successor, but Robert Cecil had corresponded secretly with James for years. The accession in March 1603 was managed within hours and without incident.

Cecil's correspondence with James, conducted under numbered ciphers and unknown to the queen, settled the terms in advance. The Council proclaimed him within eight hours of her death, and a ring was carried north as proof.

Dee chose the date of her coronation by astrology, taught her enough mathematics to follow his arguments, and advised her navigators. The favour did not extend to paying him properly.

He was consulted on the calendar reform of 1583, recommending adoption of the Gregorian correction on astronomical grounds; the bishops blocked it as a popish innovation and England kept the old calendar for another 170 years.
Lyly wrote comedies performed before the queen by boy companies and spent thirteen fruitless years petitioning her for the office of Master of the Revels.

Elizabeth delayed for months after the trial, and pressed Mary's keeper Sir Amias Paulet to act without a warrant, which he refused to do. She signed the warrant in February 1587, then prosecuted her secretary William Davison for despatching it.

Paulet replied that God forbid he should make so foul a shipwreck of his conscience. Davison was fined ten thousand marks and imprisoned in the Tower, the fine never collected, and the queen maintained for the rest of her life that the despatch had been unauthorised.

She signed the warrant, revoked it, and signed again. He was beheaded privately within the Tower in February 1601.

The story that she had given him a ring to return if he ever needed her mercy, and that it was intercepted, is a later legend with no contemporary support. What is documented is that she signed, recalled the warrant, and signed again.

The outcome was commemorated with medals bearing an inscription attributing the dispersal to a divine wind. The immediate aftermath was less favourable: thousands of seamen went unpaid and many died of typhus in the Kent ports.

The Chatham Chest, funded by deductions from seamen's pay, was set up in the aftermath by Hawkins and Drake because the crown would not provide. The victory was commemorated annually for two centuries, and the campaign entered the national self-image well before it entered the histories.
Elizabeth delayed the execution of her only duke for four months and signed the warrant three times before it was carried out.

The queen rode through the camp on 9 August 1588 with an escort and addressed the assembled troops. By that date the Armada had already been driven past the Straits and was making north, though this was not yet known at Tilbury.

The text of the speech survives only in later copies, and its exact wording is uncertain.

She was brought in by water in March 1554, refusing at first to land, and held for two months while the council looked for evidence linking her to Wyatt. She rode through the Tower again in triumph before her coronation.

She was landed at the steps in the rain on Palm Sunday and is said to have sat down on the stones and refused to go in. Wyatt exonerated her from the scaffold, and no letter in her hand was ever produced.
Elizabeth was the rebels' intended beneficiary whether or not she knew of the plan. No evidence was found, but suspicion put her in the Tower and then under house arrest at Woodstock.

Henry was nine when his mother died on her thirty-seventh birthday, and the household accounts record him inconsolable. Her Yorkist blood was half his claim to the throne.

Henry wrote to Erasmus some years afterwards that news of his mother's death had been the most hateful intelligence he had ever received. Her death in 1503, with the male line reduced to one boy of eleven, is part of the context for his later determination to secure a son.
Bacon sat in her parliaments and served as learned counsel, but never got the offices he wanted, having offended her early by opposing a subsidy.
Bacon appeared for the crown at the trial of his own patron and afterwards wrote the official account justifying the verdict.
Essex gave Bacon an estate when he could not get him office, and Bacon gave Essex political advice he consistently ignored.

Drake's raid on Cadiz in 1587 destroyed shipping and stores and delayed the Armada by a year. Philip put a price on his head; Spain called him El Draque.

The Cadiz raid destroyed some thirty ships and the seasoned barrel staves for the Armada's provisions, which meant the fleet sailed the following year with casks that leaked and food that spoiled. Drake called it singeing the King of Spain's beard.

Drake was vice-admiral, captured the Rosario on the first night after leaving the fleet in darkness to chase her, and helped choose the fireships sent in off Calais.

Taking the Rosario meant showing no stern lantern for the fleet to follow, and Frobisher accused him openly of abandoning his station for a prize. Howard declined to pursue the complaint, and the fireship attack Drake helped organise off Calais decided the campaign two days later.
The two senior English commanders of the Dutch war, they trained a generation of officers in the tactics that English armies used until the Civil War.

Walsingham controlled the beer-barrel channel through which Mary's letters passed and read everything before it was delivered. He let the plot mature until Mary endorsed the assassination in writing, then arrested everyone.

Gilbert Gifford, a seminarist turned double agent, offered Mary the channel; Thomas Phelippes deciphered every letter and forged the postscript asking for the conspirators' names. Walsingham's aim throughout was evidence against Mary rather than the arrest of Babington.

Marlowe was absent from Cambridge for extended periods, and his degree was granted in 1587 only after the Privy Council certified that he had been employed on matters concerning the queen's service. The nature of that employment is not recorded, but it is generally taken to have been intelligence work.
Walsingham pushed constantly for a more aggressive Protestant foreign policy than the queen wanted, and paid for much of his intelligence work out of his own pocket. He died in debt.

Walsingham assembled the evidence, the commission and the venue for the trial, and Mary named him from the floor as the man who had contrived her destruction.

He did not attend the execution, and the queen's subsequent anger at the warrant's despatch fell on William Davison rather than on him.

He had wanted the trial held at the Tower and in public; the queen insisted on a remote castle and a commission rather than a court. Mary's direct accusation of him from the floor drew the only personal denial he made during the proceedings.
Sidney married Walsingham's daughter Frances, and Walsingham paid the debts and the funeral when Sidney died at Zutphen.

Holbein was retained as a court painter from 1536 and produced the Whitehall mural of Henry VII, Elizabeth of York, Henry VIII and Jane Seymour. The mural was destroyed when the palace burned in 1698, and the composition survives through copies and a surviving cartoon.

He also designed plate, jewellery, book title-pages and a ceremonial clock, and drew the court in coloured chalks; some eighty of those drawings survive at Windsor. He was paid a salary of thirty pounds a year and worked on commission besides.

Arthur was born in Winchester within eight months of the wedding, and named for the British myth Henry VII wanted attached to his line. He was raised as the heir from the cradle and sent to hold the Welsh Marches at fifteen.

The choice of Winchester, believed then to be Camelot, and of the name were deliberate: the dynasty was being attached to a British past older than the Plantagenets. Arthur's death undid a decade of planning at a stroke.

Henry landed at Milford Haven in August 1485 with a force of French, Scottish and Welsh troops and gathered support crossing Wales. The battle turned on the Stanleys withholding their men and then intervening; chroniclers report the crown being recovered from the field and placed on Henry's head.

The marriage of 1486 united the Lancastrian claimant with the senior Yorkist heiress. It was the political settlement of the Wars of the Roses expressed as a wedding, and the Tudor rose was its badge.

Henry delayed the wedding until after his own coronation and his first parliament, so that his title should rest on his own claim rather than on hers. He waited a further two years before having her crowned.

Henry was the spare, raised for the church rather than the throne, and only became heir when Arthur died in 1502.

The second son had been intended for the church, which is one explanation offered for his later theological confidence. He inherited a full treasury, an unchallenged title and his brother's widow.

The accession of April 1509 was the first peaceful transfer of the English crown in almost a century, and it was greeted with relief at the end of the old king's fines and bonds.

Henry VIII opened the reign by arresting Empson and Dudley, his father's financial agents, and executing them the following year on a confected treason charge. It was a cheap way of disowning the exactions while keeping the proceeds.

Henry married his elder daughter to James IV in 1503 under the Treaty of Perpetual Peace. Later writers attribute to him the observation that if her descendants should inherit England, the greater realm would draw the lesser, though the remark is recorded only at second hand.

The act of 1534 declared that the king was and had always been Supreme Head of the Church of England, framing the change as recognition of an existing right rather than an innovation.

The accompanying Treasons Act made it capital to deny the title, which is the provision under which More and Bishop Fisher were tried.

The Act of Succession of the same year required an oath tendered across the country by local commissioners, which made the change a matter every parish had to register rather than a quarrel among bishops.

Henry pursued the annulment of his first marriage for some six years before marrying Anne in January 1533; she was crowned that June. The break with Rome was completed in the same period, and the marriage lasted three years.

Cranmer pronounced the first marriage void in May 1533, four months after the wedding and while Anne was already pregnant. The Act of Succession the following year required subjects to swear to the validity of the new marriage, which is what put More and Fisher in the Tower.

The charges of adultery with five men, including her brother, were assembled within a fortnight in May 1536, and all the accused were convicted. Historians generally regard the accusations as unfounded. Anne was beheaded on 19 May by a swordsman brought from Calais.

The tribunal that convicted her included her uncle Norfolk and her former suitor Henry Percy. Her marriage was annulled two days before the execution, which had the effect of bastardising Elizabeth while leaving the treason conviction standing.

Cromwell arranged the match for a Protestant alliance in 1540. Henry disliked her on sight, the marriage was annulled in six months, and the minister who made it went to the block.

The diplomatic case for the match evaporated within weeks as Charles V and Francis I fell out, leaving Henry with a marriage he had entered for an alliance he no longer needed. Both parties testified to non-consummation and Anne raised no objection.

Henry married her within weeks of the Cleves annulment and called her his rose without a thorn. He was forty-nine and gouty; she was probably about seventeen.

The marriage was announced on the day Cromwell was executed. She was set up with a household and jewels on a generous scale, and the king's evident renewal of spirits was remarked on by ambassadors that winter.

Cranmer passed Henry a letter detailing her past, and a new act made it treason for an unchaste woman to marry a king.

Cranmer left the letter for the king in the chapel royal at All Souls rather than deliver it in person. Culpeper and Francis Dereham were executed in December 1541, and Catherine and Lady Rochford in February 1542 by attainder rather than trial.

Henry married his brother's widow in June 1509 under a papal dispensation, and the marriage lasted twenty-four years. After repeated pregnancies produced only one surviving child, he came to argue that the dispensation had been invalid because the union contravened the prohibition in Leviticus.

She was regent in 1513 while he campaigned in France, and it was during her regency that the Scots were destroyed at Flodden. The marriage was by most accounts a working partnership for its first fifteen years.

Parr was a twice-widowed woman of thirty-one who nursed the king through his last years and acted as regent when he campaigned in France. She came close to arrest for heresy and talked her way out of it.

The heresy charge in 1546 was pressed by Gardiner and Wriothesley, who had obtained a warrant; she submitted to the king in person on the ground that she had argued theology only to distract him from his leg. Henry cancelled the arrest.

Henry took the lands of some eight hundred houses and sold most of them within a decade to pay for war in France and Scotland. The buyers became a landed class with a permanent interest in never restoring the abbeys.

The Court of Augmentations was created to administer the windfall, and land was sold at around twenty years' purchase to whoever could pay. Within a generation the buyers included most of the gentry families who sat in the Commons, which made reversal politically impossible.

The son Henry had spent thirty years and two marriages pursuing was guarded obsessively, his rooms scrubbed and his visitors screened. He was nine when he inherited.

Access to the boy was restricted, his food tasted and his rooms washed down, and he was kept from London in plague seasons. He was educated by Cheke and Cox in a firmly reformist household.

Henry's death was concealed for three days while the Seymours secured the boy and the Council. The will named sixteen executors to govern jointly, and that arrangement lasted less than a month.

The delay allowed Edward Seymour to reach the prince and secure both his person and the Council before the death was announced. The will's provision for government by sixteen executors was set aside within days in favour of a Protectorate.

Elizabeth was two when her mother was executed and she was declared illegitimate. She never spoke publicly against her father and modelled a great deal of her kingship on him.

The third Act of Succession of 1544 restored both daughters to the line without reversing their illegitimacy, an arrangement of some legal awkwardness that nonetheless governed what happened in 1553 and 1558.

The two kings and their households met near Guînes for some seventeen days of tournaments, banquets and display, housed in temporary structures of timber, canvas and glass. Chroniclers report a wrestling bout between the kings, though accounts of it are late and unreliable.

Henry took the palace from Wolsey and doubled it, adding the great hall, the kitchens and the tennis court.

The kitchens were built to feed a court of six hundred twice a day, and the great hall was worked on by night as well as day to finish it. Water was piped three miles under the Thames from Coombe Hill, an engineering undertaking unusual for a domestic building.

Holbein was sent abroad to portray prospective brides, among them Christina of Denmark and Anne of Cleves. Later accounts blamed the Cleves portrait for Henry's disappointment on meeting her, though the criticism came after the marriage had already become politically inconvenient.

The Cleves portrait is a careful likeness rather than a flattering one, and Anne's brother had also sent envoys who described her. The failure was of expectation rather than of painting, but the story attached itself to Holbein permanently.

Henry was betrothed to Jane the day after Anne Boleyn's execution and married her ten days later. She was a Seymour, conservative in religion, and had served both previous queens; her motto was Bound to Obey and Serve.

She was never crowned, the ceremony being postponed first for plague and then indefinitely. Her surviving political act was to intercede for the northern rebels in 1536, which Henry rebuffed with a reminder of what had happened to his last queen.

Henry mistrusted his sister's Scottish loyalties and her divorce, and warred against her son James V. His invasion of 1542 ended at Solway Moss and left her granddaughter Mary on the Scottish throne within weeks.

Mary was the treasured only child until the annulment, when she was declared a bastard, separated from her mother and made to wait on her infant half-sister. She submitted in 1536 and never forgave the men who made her.

She was made to sign an acknowledgement that her parents' marriage had been unlawful and that she was illegitimate, a submission she later told the imperial ambassador she had made under duress and did not regard as binding.

Henry authorised Norfolk to promise whatever was necessary and then repudiated it, calling the pilgrims rude commons of one of the most brute shires in the realm. A fresh disturbance in 1537 gave him the pretext to hang the leaders.

He wrote to Norfolk that he should cause such dreadful execution upon a good number of the inhabitants as they might be a fearful spectacle. Around 200 were executed in 1537, including Aske, hanged in chains at York.

Cromwell was arrested at the Council table in June 1540, attainted without trial, and executed on the day the king married Catherine Howard. Henry blamed his councillors for it within a year.

The attainder listed heresy and treason together, charges that contradicted each other and were supported by no trial. Cromwell wrote to the king from the Tower asking for mercy and ending with the words mercy, mercy, mercy; he was executed on 28 July 1540.

More declined to swear the oath of succession and refused to give reasons, maintaining that the law could not punish silence. He was convicted largely on evidence given by Richard Rich, which More denied, and was beheaded on Tower Hill in July 1535.

Rich testified to a conversation in the Tower in which More was alleged to have denied parliament's competence to make the king head of the church. More's reply in court, that the jury should weigh which of the two of them was more likely to be lying, did not save him.

Foxe records Latimer's words to Ridley at the stake, about lighting a candle in England that would never be put out. The sentence became the most widely quoted passage in Acts and Monuments and shaped later Protestant memory of the reign.

Bishop and preacher, they were tried together at Oxford, held in the same Bocardo prison, and burned back to back at the same stake in October 1555.

Ridley was the theologian and Latimer the preacher, and each converted the other on a point: Ridley brought Latimer to a Reformed view of the eucharist, and Latimer's plain style influenced Ridley's preaching. They were tried together and refused to answer separately.

Mary raised East Anglia from Framlingham, the Council in London changed sides within days, and Jane's regime collapsed without a battle. It is the one moment in the century when popular support for the legitimate heir simply overruled the men holding the capital.

Mary was warned in time to avoid arrest and rode to Kenninghall and then Framlingham, proclaiming herself queen and gathering gentry and commons in numbers Northumberland could not match. The Council in London proclaimed her on 19 July, nine days after Jane.

Jane went to the Tower to be proclaimed queen and never left it. She was held for six months and executed after Wyatt's rebellion made her a standing danger.

She and Guildford Dudley were tried and condemned in November 1553, and the sentence was not expected to be carried out. Wyatt's rising, and her father's part in it, changed that; she refused Feckenham's attempts to convert her and was executed on 12 February 1554.
Jane died of puerperal fever twelve days after delivering the son Henry had waited nearly thirty years for.

Edward was born in the queen's apartments there in October 1537, and Jane died in the same rooms twelve days later of the infection that followed.

The birth on 12 October 1537 was followed by a christening of great ceremony at which Mary stood as godmother and the four-year-old Elizabeth was carried in the procession. Jane received guests from her bed and died on 24 October.

Dee supplied cartographic and legal arguments for an English title in the north Atlantic, based on claims of earlier discovery, while Hakluyt assembled the voyage narratives. Their work together provided much of the intellectual case for English colonisation.

Dee's argument was juridical and cartographic, Hakluyt's documentary: between them they supplied a claim of right and a body of evidence that voyages had been made. Both worked for the same patrons and to the same end.
Northumberland governed through the Council rather than as Protector, stabilised the currency and the finances, and drove the Prayer Book of 1552 through.

Northumberland married his son Guildford to Jane in May 1553, weeks before Edward VI's death, and had her proclaimed queen in July. When support moved to Mary he abandoned the attempt at Cambridge; he conformed to Catholicism before his execution without effect on the sentence.

Jane herself refused the crown at first and, having accepted it, refused to make Guildford king. Northumberland's error was to leave London to take Mary in the field, which left the Council free to change sides behind him.
Northumberland surrendered at Cambridge, was brought back through crowds that shouted for Mary, and heard mass publicly on the scaffold in a failed bid to save his family.

Foxe gathered depositions, letters and eyewitness accounts in exile and after, and published in English in 1563. The book ran to millions of words and was revised through four editions in his lifetime.

He worked from the registers of the London and Canterbury dioceses, from letters smuggled out of prisons, and from survivors who came to him after 1559. The 1570 edition doubled the length and extended the narrative back to the early Church.

Foxe gathered depositions, letters and eyewitness accounts of the burnings and published them in English in 1563. The book presented the executions within a long history of the Church, and it shaped English accounts of Mary's reign for generations.

Kinsmen from Plymouth, they sailed together on the 1567 to 1568 voyage that ended when Spanish forces attacked their ships at San Juan de Ulúa, an episode both cited for years afterwards. They died within weeks of each other in 1595 and 1596 on a final Caribbean expedition.

Hawkins commanded and Drake sailed as a junior officer on the third slaving voyage of 1567. When the Spanish attacked the ships at San Juan de Ulúa under a flag of truce, only two of six vessels escaped; both men treated it thereafter as licensing everything they subsequently did against Spain.

Hawkins commanded the Victory in the 1588 campaign, one of the race-built galleons produced by the rebuilding programme he had directed as Treasurer of the Navy since 1577. He was knighted at sea during the Channel fighting.

He also pressed, without success, for the fleet to be sent to blockade the Spanish coast rather than wait in the Channel.
Norreys was the professional whose experience Essex leaned on and resented, and the two campaigned together in Normandy and Brittany against the Catholic League.

Whitgift required subscription to three articles affirming the royal supremacy, the Prayer Book and the Thirty-Nine Articles, and used the Court of High Commission to enforce it. Several hundred ministers were suspended, though many later conformed.

Burghley wrote to him that the articles resembled the Roman inquisition and that he found them so curiously penned that the clergy could not answer them without peril. Whitgift had the queen's backing and did not give way.
The queen called him her little black husband and backed his campaign against nonconformity without reservation.
Lettice's son inherited his stepfather Leicester's place at court and his mother's exclusion from it, and spent much of his career trying to get her received again.
Margaret's third husband was Lord Stanley, whose decision to change sides at the critical moment gave her son the battle.

Margaret was thirteen when Henry was born and a widow before it. For twenty-eight years she worked to keep his claim alive, and once he was king she signed herself Margaret R.

She had been married at twelve to Edmund Tudor, who died of plague before the birth, and the delivery at thirteen appears to have left her unable to bear another child. Her later marriages were political arrangements that kept her within reach of events.
James was Margaret's great-grandson twice over, descending from her through both his father and his mother. That double Tudor descent was the whole legal basis of the union of the crowns in 1603.

Margaret's marriage to James IV put Tudor blood into the Scottish royal line; Mary was her granddaughter. That descent is exactly what made Mary the Catholic heir to England.

Henry VIII's will had attempted to exclude the Scottish line from the English succession in favour of the descendants of his younger sister, which is where Jane Grey's title came from. Whether a will could override common-law inheritance was never settled in court.

Both built careers on the idea of a passage to Cathay round the top of America, Gilbert arguing it in print and Frobisher sailing three times to look for it.

Gilbert's Discourse of a Discoverie for a New Passage to Cataia circulated in manuscript for a decade before publication in 1576, and Frobisher's first voyage sailed in the same year on the strength of the argument. Michael Lok, who financed it, had read Gilbert closely.

Frobisher commanded the Triumph, the largest ship in the English fleet, and held the inshore station off Portland against the Armada's right wing.

The Triumph and five armed merchantmen were cut off inshore off Portland and had to be towed clear by their boats in a calm before the Spanish could close. Frobisher was knighted at sea by Howard immediately afterwards.

Mary died childless in November 1558, having failed to secure a Catholic heir, and the crown passed to the half-sister she had imprisoned. Elizabeth kept a good deal of Mary's administration and reversed nearly all of her religion.

Mary acknowledged the succession only in her last weeks, and asked that her religion be maintained, which it was not. The transition was managed smoothly because Cecil had prepared it and because the political nation had had enough of reversals.

Seventeen years apart, and divided by their mothers, their religion and the legitimacy of each other's birth. Mary imprisoned Elizabeth after Wyatt's rising and could never quite bring herself to destroy her.

The two false pregnancies that ended Mary's hopes of a Catholic heir left Elizabeth as the certain successor, which is the main reason she survived. Mary sent to her repeatedly for a promise to maintain the old religion, and never got one.
Latimer was tried at Oxford with Ridley and Cranmer and burned in October 1555 outside the town wall.

The heresy laws were revived by parliament in 1554 and the first burnings took place at Smithfield in February 1555. Mary did not alter the policy, despite advice that it was strengthening rather than weakening Protestant opinion.

Renard, the imperial ambassador, and Philip's own confessor both advised against the burnings on the ground that they were counterproductive. The parish accounts show communities buying the faggots and the stake, so that the cost of each execution fell on the neighbours who watched it.
Ridley had preached at Paul's Cross for Jane Grey's title and against both of Henry's daughters as bastards, which made his case hopeless before it began.

The marriage treaty of 1554 gave Philip the title of king but almost no power, and the match was deeply unpopular. He spent barely fourteen months in England, there were no children, and it dragged England into war with France and the loss of Calais.

Parliament required a treaty barring Philip from English office, from taking the queen abroad, and from succeeding her if she died childless. He was styled king, appeared with her on the coinage, and had no independent power in England.

Cranmer had pronounced the annulment of Mary's mother's marriage, and the sentence against him stood despite the six submissions he signed. At his execution in March 1556 he withdrew the recantations and held his right hand in the fire.

He was degraded from orders in a ceremony of deliberate humiliation before the burning, and expected to read a final submission from the stage at St Mary's. He read a repudiation instead, was pulled down, and went to the stake at once.
Mary refused to leave London, made a direct appeal at the Guildhall, and the city held. The rising failed at Ludgate, but it hardened her regime considerably.

Mary's reply to Babington approved the design against Elizabeth, and a forged postscript asked for the conspirators' names. That letter was read aloud at her trial and she could not explain it away.

The forged postscript was added by Phelippes in a hand matching the cipher clerk's, and was the one element the prosecution could not have obtained honestly. The letter itself, without it, was sufficient: Mary had approved the design in writing.

Two queens who never met and corresponded for twenty years. Mary's claim made her the natural focus of every Catholic plot, and Elizabeth's refusal to name an heir kept that claim alive.

Elizabeth refused repeatedly to meet her, and refused equally to recognise her as heir or to exclude her. Nineteen years of custody without trial or charge was a solution to a problem that admitted of no lawful answer.

Mary was moved to Fotheringhay in September 1586, tried in the great hall in October before a commission of thirty-six peers and councillors, and executed there on 8 February 1587.

She was refused her own counsel and denied sight of the letters used against her, and she declined to recognise the court's jurisdiction over an anointed foreign queen.

James was thirteen months old when his mother was forced to abdicate, and he was raised by her enemies. He accepted her execution with a formal protest and no more.

He had no memory of her, and his tutors were paid by the men who had deposed her. When she proposed a joint sovereignty in the 1580s he declined, and he accepted an English pension instead.
Norfolk was persuaded that marrying the Scottish queen would settle the succession, and Ridolfi turned that into a plot involving Spanish troops.
Parker was consecrated under the new settlement in 1559 and then had to enforce it, issuing the Advertisements on vestments that started the first Puritan quarrel.

Convocation ordered copies of Acts and Monuments to be placed in cathedral churches and in the houses of senior clergy, giving the book a semi-official standing. Parker also lent Foxe manuscripts from his collection of pre-Conquest English texts.

Parker's own antiquarian project ran in parallel: he was assembling Anglo-Saxon manuscripts to demonstrate that the pre-Conquest English church had been married, vernacular and independent of Rome, which supplied the settlement with a usable history.
Parker took the archbishopric reluctantly and spent it holding a middle line between returning exiles who wanted more reform and parishes that wanted less.

The whole plan depended on these two joining forces, and they had no reliable way of communicating across the Channel. Parma's barges could not come out past the Dutch flyboats, and the fleet had nowhere to wait.

Communication depended on pinnaces carrying letters into ports that Dutch blockading squadrons patrolled, so messages took days and several never arrived. Medina Sidonia anchored off Calais on 6 August still without confirmation that Parma could embark, which he could not.

He wrote to Philip on appointment that he had no experience of naval war and was habitually seasick, and asked to be excused; the king refused. He held the fleet in its defensive formation through the Channel, and brought roughly half of it home.

His orders were rigid: to sail to Flanders and escort Parma's army, not to seek battle or attempt a landing on his own account. Following them exactly was the one course that could not succeed, and he followed them.

Hilliard painted the queen without shadow, on her insistence, producing the flat radiant mask that became the official face of the reign.

He recorded her instruction that portraits should be made in open alley in the garden, in plain light without shadow, so that the modelling of the face was flattened out. The result was less a likeness than a device, reproduced by workshops for the rest of the reign.

Hilliard's miniature of Raleigh, all pearls and black and white, is the image that fixed the courtier's self-presentation for posterity.

Raleigh was among the courtiers who used the miniature as a political object, given as a token and worn visibly. Hilliard's images of him carry the pearls and the black-and-white colouring that were the queen's own device, a way of advertising favour.

Ridley's execution in October 1555 was prolonged, and Foxe's account of it circulated widely. Along with Latimer and Cranmer he became known as one of the Oxford Martyrs, commemorated by a memorial erected on the site in the nineteenth century.

His brother-in-law heaped on more wood in an attempt to hasten it, which had the opposite effect. Foxe's account, illustrated with a woodcut, was among the most reproduced images in English print for two centuries.

Henslowe's companies held the Marlowe repertory and his diary records the takings for Faustus and The Jew of Malta, which is much of what we know about their popularity.

The diary records repeated performances of The Jew of Malta over several seasons with the takings for each, which is why more is known about the popularity of Marlowe's plays than about the audience for anyone else's.

Philip planned the campaign in detail from Madrid, insisting the fleet meet Parma's army off Flanders without ever securing a deep-water port for the rendezvous. The plan's central flaw was his own.

He rejected proposals to seize a deep-water port such as Flushing first, and dismissed warnings from both commanders that the rendezvous was impracticable, writing that the enterprise was God's and would therefore prosper. When it failed he remarked that he had sent his ships against men, not the winds.

Spenser dedicated The Shepheardes Calender to Sidney and put him into later poetry as Astrophel. The two were part of the same militant Protestant literary circle around Leicester.

Spenser's Astrophel, an elegy published in 1595, made Sidney into the presiding figure of a Protestant literary myth. The Areopagus, the supposed circle around them experimenting with classical metres in English, may be more a scholarly construction than a real society.

Both served in the Netherlands under Leicester in the campaign of 1585 to 1586, and both were present in the fighting around Zutphen where Sidney received his wound. Vere afterwards commanded the English forces there for more than a decade.

The bull of February 1570 followed rather than preceded the Northern Rising, and arrived too late to assist it. Its practical effect was to place English Catholics under suspicion of disloyalty, and it was cited in the treason statutes passed in 1571 and after.

Gregory XIII issued an explanation in 1580 that Catholics need not act on the deposition while it could not be enforced, but the qualification arrived a decade late and made little practical difference to how the penal laws were applied.

Pius issued the bull without consulting the Catholic powers, who thought it reckless. It declared Elizabeth a heretic, deposed her, and forbade her subjects to obey her.

The bull was drawn up after an inquiry in Rome at which English exiles gave evidence, and it was issued as a judicial sentence rather than a political manoeuvre, which is why it made no allowance for the position it left English Catholics in.

Pole answered the king's request for an opinion with a violent attack on the supremacy, then took a cardinal's hat. Henry could not reach him, so he executed his mother, the Countess of Salisbury, instead.

The Countess of Salisbury was held in the Tower for two years and executed in 1541 at nearly seventy, on no charge that was ever tried. Pole said afterwards that he was the son of a martyr.

Pole returned in 1554 as papal legate and absolved the realm of schism, then became Archbishop of Canterbury after Cranmer's burning. He died within hours of the queen he had come back to serve.

His legatine synod of 1556 planned seminaries in every diocese for training parish clergy, anticipating the Tridentine decrees by several years. None was built before the reign ended, and the programme died with him.
Burbage created the part and was still playing it in his forties, and an elegy at his death listed the young prince among the roles that died with him.

Burbage and his brother Cuthbert held half the shares in the playhouse, with the other half split among Shakespeare and four fellow actors. It was their father James who had built the Theatre whose timbers became the Globe.

The dismantling in December 1598 was done at night over the Christmas holiday while the ground landlord was out of London, and the company later argued in court that the timber was theirs because the building was. The judges agreed.

They worked together for twenty years, and the great tragic roles were written for Burbage's particular gifts. Shakespeare left him money for a memorial ring.

The parts written for him lengthen and darken over twenty years, from Richard III to Lear, which is as close as the period comes to a record of an actor's development. He was also a painter, and a portrait at Dulwich is attributed to him.

Grenville had proposed a Pacific voyage in 1574 that the crown declined to authorise, and the project passed instead to Drake. The two were rival figures in West Country maritime enterprise and in the Irish plantations, though they served the same interests against Spain.

Grenville's 1574 petition for a southern voyage was refused on diplomatic grounds and the project revived three years later under Drake, who sailed with the queen's secret backing. Grenville was left to the Irish plantations and, later, to Roanoke.

Hakluyt collected and printed Gilbert's Discourse on the North-West Passage, and used the Newfoundland voyage as the founding precedent for an English claim in America.

Hakluyt's own first publication, Divers Voyages of 1582, was dedicated to the promotion of Gilbert's project and printed maps and narratives assembled to demonstrate that the passage existed and that England had a title to the coast.
Cecil did the secretary's work for years before he was given the title, and the queen kept him waiting deliberately. By the last years of the reign he controlled access to her almost entirely.

Cecil conducted a secret correspondence with Edinburgh under cipher for the last years of the reign, coaching James on how to approach the English and ensuring the succession was settled before Elizabeth died.

The letters were unsigned and numbered, Cecil being 10 and James 30, and their discovery would have been treason. He coached James against promising too much to English Catholics and against arriving with a Scottish following.
Essex wanted to be a general and demanded commands the queen thought beyond him. The Cadiz raid made his reputation and the Irish command destroyed it.

Essex was some thirty-three years younger than the queen and enjoyed a familiarity at court that his rivals resented, sustained through letters of elaborate devotion and periods of ostentatious withdrawal. The relationship broke down in 1599 when he returned from Ireland without leave and entered her private chamber unannounced.

Deserting his Irish command, confined and ruined, Essex marched into the City with two hundred men expecting London to rise. It did not, and the whole affair was over by nightfall.

He had held the queen's Secretary and two other councillors hostage in his own house, then left them there. Southampton was condemned with him and reprieved; four others were executed. Essex asked to die privately rather than on Tower Hill.
The two men divided the court between war party and peace party, and Cecil won by staying in office while Essex went to Ireland.
Essex was brought from Lambeth after the rising, tried in Westminster Hall by his peers, and beheaded on Tower Green in the last such execution held there.

Spenser entered Leicester's household about 1579 and dedicated The Shepheardes Calender to Sidney from within that circle. The connection placed him close to the militant Protestant grouping at court.

A perceived criticism of the proposed French marriage in Mother Hubberds Tale is generally thought to have cost him further advancement in England.

They had known each other since childhood and were both in the Tower in 1554. The death of his wife Amy Robsart in 1560 made marriage politically impossible, and he stayed the closest man to her for thirty years regardless.

Amy Robsart was found dead at the foot of a staircase at Cumnor Place in September 1560; the inquest returned misadventure, but the suspicion was permanent and the marriage became impossible at exactly the point it had become plausible. He was made Earl of Leicester in 1564 and offered, remarkably, as a husband for Mary, Queen of Scots.
Leicester married Lettice secretly in 1578. When Elizabeth found out she banished the bride permanently and never entirely forgave him.

Sidney was Leicester's nephew and, until his uncle fathered a son, heir presumptive to the earldom. He served under him as Governor of Flushing in the Netherlands expedition and took his fatal wound there in 1586.

Leicester's late marriage and the birth of a son in 1581 displaced Sidney from the inheritance; the boy died at three. Sidney's appointment to Flushing came through his uncle, and he was buried at St Paul's at Walsingham's expense after a funeral of unprecedented scale for a commoner.

Leicester organised the Tilbury camp and arranged the queen's review of the troops. He died a few weeks later, and Elizabeth kept his last letter in a box by her bed.

He died at Cornbury in September 1588 on his way to take the waters at Buxton. Elizabeth wrote his last letter over with the words His Last Letter and kept it in a casket beside her bed, where it was found after her death.
Cecil thought Leicester's ambitions dangerous and worked to prevent the marriage; Leicester thought Cecil timid abroad. They quarrelled for thirty years and cooperated for most of them.

Ascham taught Elizabeth Greek and Latin in her teens and boasted of her fluency. Her habit of answering ambassadors in Latin on the spot dates from those lessons.

He described her programme in a letter to Sturm: mornings in Greek with the New Testament and Sophocles, afternoons in Latin with Cicero and Livy, and double translation out of the language and back again. She read with him for about two years.

Ascham kept the post of Latin secretary through Mary's reign despite his Protestantism, writing her diplomatic correspondence without being asked to change his religion.

The Scholemaster grew out of a dinner conversation at Windsor in 1563 about boys running away from Eton to escape beating. His argument that fear produces neither learning nor honesty was unusual enough to still be quoted three centuries later.

Gardiner pressed for the revival of the heresy laws and presided over the early examinations, then drew back as it became clear the burnings were making converts rather than preventing them.

He had wanted a policy of a few exemplary executions among the leaders, and the burning of obscure artisans in numbers was not what he had argued for. By the autumn of 1555 he had withdrawn from the examinations entirely.
Released from the Tower on Mary's accession and made Lord Chancellor, Gardiner drove the repeal of the Edwardian legislation and negotiated the Spanish marriage treaty he privately disliked.
Gardiner spent the whole of Edward's reign in the Tower for refusing to accept the Protectorate's religious changes, and was deprived of Winchester in 1551.

Cranmer compiled the 1549 book from Latin, Lutheran and Sarum sources into a single English liturgy, then revised it in 1552 in a firmly Protestant direction. Its collects and its cadences are still audible in English prose.

The 1549 book was conservative enough in its wording to be read in a traditional sense, which was the point: it had to be usable in parishes that had not changed their minds. The 1552 revision removed that latitude, stripping the eucharistic words of any suggestion of sacrifice.
With a Protestant boy on the throne Cranmer could finally legislate the doctrine he had held privately for years, issuing the Prayer Books, the Ordinal and the Forty-Two Articles in six years.
Cranmer rose by suggesting that the universities of Europe, not the pope, should rule on the king's marriage. As archbishop he then annulled that marriage, and two more besides.
Cranmer was the most valuable of all the victims and the most compromised, having sworn obedience to the crown in religion and then met a crown that ordered him back to Rome.

They argued the eucharist in print and in council for twenty years, Gardiner defending the real presence and Cranmer dismantling it. Each in turn imprisoned the other's cause when the throne changed hands.

Gardiner's Detection of the Devil's Sophistry and Cranmer's Defence of the True and Catholic Doctrine were answered by each other in successive volumes, an exchange conducted while one of them was in the Tower. It is the fullest doctrinal argument of the English Reformation.

Cromwell drafted the supremacy legislation and the treason act that gave it teeth, and organised the administration of the oath throughout the country.

As Vicegerent in Spirituals he then exercised the new authority on the king's behalf, ranking above the archbishops in convocation.

He was a layman exercising jurisdiction over the whole English church, an arrangement without precedent, and he used it to issue injunctions requiring an English Bible in every parish and the keeping of registers of baptisms, marriages and burials.

As Vicegerent in Spirituals, Cromwell ordered the visitations that produced the evidence, drafted the statutes, and ran the commissions that took the surrenders. The proceeds went into the crown's hands and out again into the gentry's.

The Valor Ecclesiasticus of 1535 surveyed every ecclesiastical income in England in under a year, an administrative achievement in itself, and the visitation reports that followed were written to justify a decision already taken.

Cromwell supplied the legal machinery of the break with Rome and governed through statute rather than prerogative, carrying the supremacy, the treason act and the dissolution through parliament. He reorganised the royal household departments into something closer to a system of state offices.

He rose from the Council to Master of the Rolls, Lord Privy Seal and Vicegerent within seven years, and was made Earl of Essex three months before his fall. Historians have argued for decades over how far the administrative changes were a deliberate revolution in government.

Norfolk represented the old nobility and the old religion, Cromwell the new men and reform. Norfolk helped bring him down in 1540 and enjoyed the victory for exactly six years before his own family fell.

Gresham raised and refinanced crown loans on the Antwerp exchange and advised on the 1560 recoinage that withdrew the debased currency of the previous two reigns. He argued for reducing the crown's dependence on foreign lenders.

The recoinage called in the debased money at a discount and reissued it at proper fineness, a technically difficult operation completed within a year that restored confidence in English currency and, unusually, showed the crown a profit.

Gresham's long series of letters to Cecil reports on credit conditions in Antwerp, the movement of bullion, and the politics of the Netherlands, and Cecil used him as the government's principal source in the money market.

Their correspondence underpinned the 1560 recoinage and the crown's gradual withdrawal from foreign borrowing.

Norfolk brought his niece to court in 1539 and supported her advancement, as he had earlier supported that of his other niece Anne Boleyn. He took no part in her defence once the allegations were laid, and sat among those who condemned her.

Norfolk commanded at Flodden's aftermath, in France and against the northern rebels, and pushed two of his nieces into the king's bed. Service and kinship together kept him at the centre of the reign for forty years.

Norfolk faced a rebel host far larger than his own, negotiated a pardon he had no intention of keeping, and hanged the leaders once the movement dispersed.

His force was outnumbered perhaps six to one, and he wrote to the king that he would make whatever promises were necessary and answer for it afterwards. The Doncaster agreement of December 1536 offered a free pardon and a parliament at York; neither was honoured.
The dukedom skipped a generation: the fourth duke's father, the poet Earl of Surrey, was executed in 1547, so the boy was raised by John Foxe and inherited from his grandfather.
Condemned for treason in January 1547, Norfolk was saved because Henry VIII died the night before the execution. He stayed in the Tower for the whole of Edward's reign and was released by Mary.
Norfolk was sent there first in 1569 for the Scottish marriage scheme, released to house arrest, and returned in 1571 when the Ridolfi correspondence was found under a doormat at Howard House.
More would not swear to the oath and would not say why, arguing that the law could not punish silence. The court decided otherwise.

Erasmus recommended Holbein to More, who received him in Chelsea on his first English visit in 1526 and introduced him to a circle of humanist and mercantile sitters.

The resulting group portrait of More's household was the first of its kind painted in England; the original is lost and the composition is known from a preparatory drawing and copies.

More's letter to Erasmus reported that the painter was a wonderful artist but that he doubted England would prove as fertile ground as he hoped. Holbein went home to Basel in 1528 and returned in 1532 to find More out of favour and his circle dispersed.

More succeeded Wolsey as Chancellor in 1529 and resigned in 1532 as soon as the church submitted to the king.

He had told the king early that if his head would win him a castle in France it would not fail to go. He accepted the chancellorship on the understanding that he need not be involved in the annulment.
More was held for fifteen months, writing the Dialogue of Comfort, while the Act of Supremacy made his silence indefensible.
The Protector's brother resented being left out of power and schemed to control the young king personally. Somerset signed his death warrant, and the fratricide badly damaged his own standing.

Seymour was arrested in January 1549 after being found at night near the king's apartments; the guard dog was reportedly shot. He was condemned by act of attainder rather than by trial, no court having been willing to hear the evidence.

As papal legate Wolsey was supposed to be able to deliver the annulment from within the church. The legatine court at Blackfriars was revoked to Rome, and his failure ended his career.

The Blackfriars court of 1529 was the only occasion on which a reigning king and queen of England appeared before a court in their own realm. Campeggio adjourned it for the Roman vacation and it never resumed.
Wolsey organised the whole spectacle, down to the seating, the tents and the order of jousting, as a demonstration of English importance in Europe.

Wolsey acquired the manor in 1514 and built a residence on a scale unusual for a subject, with lodgings for a large household and for visiting royalty. He transferred it to Henry VIII in 1529 as his position was failing.

He leased the manor from the Knights Hospitaller in 1514 and built lodgings for a household of five hundred, with a suite kept for the king. Skelton's satire on him made the comparison with royal state explicit, and the gift of the palace in 1529 did not save him.

As Lord Chancellor, cardinal and papal legate, Wolsey directed domestic administration and foreign policy for roughly fifteen years, allowing the young king to leave the routine of government to him. His position depended entirely on retaining the king's confidence.

He held Winchester and the abbacy of St Albans in commendam alongside York, and his income approached the crown's own. The legatine authority let him bypass Canterbury, which stored up resentment among the bishops who later did nothing to save him.

Cromwell learned government in Wolsey's service, dissolving small monasteries to fund the cardinal's colleges. When Wolsey fell, Cromwell defended him in parliament and then took his place in the king's business.

Cromwell's defence of his fallen master in the Commons was a considerable risk that established his reputation for competence and nerve. He carried Wolsey's methods into royal service, including the use of survey and commission.

More took the Great Seal in October 1529 as the cardinal fell, and became the first layman in generations to hold it. He accepted knowing the matter that had destroyed his predecessor was still unresolved.
Wyatt served as ambassador to the emperor and was twice arrested at home, once in 1536 when his supposed connection to Anne Boleyn made him dangerous.
From a Tower window in May 1536 Wyatt may have watched Anne Boleyn's execution; the poem beginning with the ringing of the bell is usually read that way.

Marlowe's lyric The Passionate Shepherd to His Love was answered by The Nymph's Reply to the Shepherd, printed as Raleigh's in England's Helicon in 1600. The two moved in overlapping circles of court patronage and speculative discussion, and both were named in the 1593 depositions alleging irreligion at Raleigh's table.

The association was later used against both men, and it remains one of the few documented literary connections between them.

Raleigh arrived at court in 1581 and was showered with monopolies, wine licences and Irish land. His secret marriage to one of her maids of honour in 1592 ended the favour abruptly and sent them both to the Tower.

Elizabeth Throckmorton was a gentlewoman of the privy chamber, and the offence was the secrecy and the breach of the queen's control over her women rather than the marriage itself. Raleigh was never fully restored, and the queen never received his wife again.

Raleigh was Spenser's neighbour in Munster, brought him to court to present the poem to the queen, and contributed a commendatory sonnet. He appears inside the allegory as the Shepherd of the Ocean.

Spenser's Colin Clouts Come Home Againe describes the visit and the journey to court in 1589, and the prefatory letter to Raleigh printed with the poem is the fullest statement Spenser made of what the allegory was for.
Gilbert was Raleigh's elder half-brother and the man who first argued for English colonies in the north-west.

Dee advised Raleigh's captains on navigation and supplied the argument that prior discovery gave England a legal title in the north Atlantic.

Dee's Brytanici Imperii Limites assembled the legal case that Madoc and the Cabots had established a prior English title in the north Atlantic, which was precisely the argument a coloniser needed against Spanish claims of papal donation.
Grenville commanded the fleet that carried Raleigh's first colonists to Roanoke in 1585 and returned with supplies the year after.

Hakluyt drafted the Discourse of Western Planting for Raleigh's colonial project and put it before the queen in 1584.

The Discourse of Western Planting was written for private presentation rather than publication, arguing that colonies would employ the idle poor, supply naval stores, provide bases against the Spanish treasure fleets and open a market for English cloth. It got Raleigh no money from the queen.

The two competed through the 1590s for military commands, monopolies and access to the queen, and their followers formed opposing court groupings. Raleigh was present as Captain of the Guard at Essex's execution in 1601, and was criticised at the time for his conduct there.

Raleigh was confined briefly in 1592 over his secret marriage to Elizabeth Throckmorton, and again from 1603 to 1616 under a treason conviction. During the second imprisonment he wrote the first volume of his History of the World.

He was released in 1616 to seek a gold mine in Guiana on condition of not provoking Spain. His men burned a Spanish settlement, his son was killed, and the old 1603 sentence was revived to satisfy Madrid. He was executed at Westminster in October 1618.

Byrd remained a Gentleman of the Chapel Royal throughout the reign and retained the printing patent granted to him and Thomas Tallis in 1575, despite being repeatedly presented as a recusant in the 1580s and 1590s.

Cecil managed the settlement bills through a hostile House of Lords in 1559, timing the arrest of two bishops to get the numbers. The church of England as it stood for centuries was largely his parliamentary carpentry.

The Lords were the obstacle, with the Marian bishops voting as a bloc. Cecil had two of them committed to the Tower for contempt after a staged disputation at Westminster, and the bills passed the upper house by three votes.
Burghley pushed the trial forward once the letters were in hand, drafting the commission and managing the parliamentary pressure that made Elizabeth's refusal untenable.

Appointed Secretary on the first day of the reign, Cecil served her for forty years and told her when she was wrong. Their partnership, quarrelsome and unbroken, is the spine of the Elizabethan state.

She made him Lord Treasurer in 1572 and ennobled him, but never let him have his way on the two questions he cared most about: the succession and intervention abroad. He submitted written memoranda arguing both for forty years.
They disagreed about how far to provoke Spain but worked as a single machine on security, running the interrogations, the cipher work and the case against Mary Stuart together.

Cecil regarded Mary as an existential threat from the moment she landed in England and worked for eighteen years to have her removed. He drafted the Bond of Association and pushed the trial commission through.

The Bond of Association, drafted after William of Orange's assassination, bound its signatories to kill anyone in whose interest an attempt on the queen was made — aimed at Mary whether or not she knew of a plot. Elizabeth had the statutory version softened.
Burghley trained his younger son in government from boyhood and manoeuvred him into the secretaryship, creating something close to a dynasty of ministers.

Supporters of Essex paid the Chamberlain's Men forty shillings to revive Richard II, a play including the deposition of a monarch, on the eve of the rising. The company was examined and accepted to have acted as commercial players; they performed at court the night before Essex's execution.

Shakespeare rewrote an older revenge play into something that keeps stopping to think. The text survives in three markedly different versions, and no one is certain which is closest to what the Globe actually staged.

The 1603 quarto is roughly half the length of the 1604 one and reorders the soliloquies; it is generally taken to be a memorial reconstruction. The Folio cuts some 230 lines present in the second quarto and adds about 70 of its own.

Shakespeare was one of the housekeepers who owned the Globe outright, which is where his money came from rather than from writing. He wrote for its specific stage: no scenery, daylight, an audience on three sides.

The sharing arrangement was devised because the company had lost the Theatre's ground lease and could not afford a landlord again. A housekeeper's share paid several times what writing did, and it is the reason Shakespeare could buy New Place and retire to it.
